title: Classical experimental tests of general relativity
one_line_summary: Derives and confronts with data the four solar-system tests of general relativity (gravitational redshift, perihelion advance, light deflection, radar time delay), argues from the Einstein equivalence principle that gravity must be a metric theory, recasts the tests in the two-parameter PPN (beta, gamma) language, and closes Part C with a chronology and a cautious rubber-sheet/embedding-diagram picture of curved space-time.
role_in_book: Final chapter of Part C. Chapter 15 produced the Schwarzschild metric; this chapter cashes it in observationally, reusing the variational geodesic method of Chapter 7 and the weak-field limit of Chapter 10, and revisiting the equivalence principle of Chapter 9 in its experimentally motivated 'Einstein' form. It is the book's first sustained contact with measurement, and it sets up Part D (effective potential, ISCO and photon sphere appear as exercises and embedding diagrams preview black-hole geometry) and Part E (binary-pulsar orbital decay and the ripple picture of gravitational waves).

assumed_background.topic: Schwarzschild line element in Schwarzschild coordinates, and the geometric mass m = GM/c^2
General static spherically symmetric line element with two free functions of r
Geodesics from the Lagrangian K = (1/2) g_ab x'^a x'^b and the Euler-Lagrange equations
Weak-field limit g_00 = 1 + 2 phi / c^2 linking the metric to the Newtonian potential
Weak and strong forms of the principle of equivalence; Mach's principle and Brans-Dicke motivation
Proper time along a world line, timelike versus null curves, affine parameter
Newton's laws, universal gravitation, angular momentum, energy in central-force motion
Plane polar coordinates with unit vectors R-hat and phi-hat and their time derivatives
Linear second-order ODEs with constant coefficients, particular integrals, resonance
Taylor expansion in a small parameter and elementary integrals (log and inverse cosh forms)
Conic sections in polar form: eccentricity, semi-latus rectum, focus
E = mc^2, Doppler shift, quantized atomic energy levels, photons
Solar system scales, eclipses, quasars and galaxies as light sources

learning_objectives: Reader can argue from energy conservation (the bucket-chain perpetual-motion paradox) that light climbing out of a gravitational field must lose frequency.

Reader can derive the redshift ratio nu_2/nu_1 = sqrt(g_00(x_1)/g_00(x_2)) for static observers in a static space-time, justify the equality of coordinate-time crest intervals, and reduce it to (phi_1 - phi_2)/c^2 in the weak field.

Reader can explain why gravitational redshift tests the equivalence principle rather than the field equations, and describe how Pound-Rebka used the Mossbauer effect and a Doppler compensation to measure a 10^-15 shift.

Reader can state the three clauses of the Einstein equivalence principle, name the experiments supporting each clause, and explain the plausibility argument that leads from them to the postulates of a metric theory of gravity.
Reader can solve the Newtonian Kepler problem via Binet's equation in u = 1/R and reduce the two-body problem to a one-body problem with reduced mass.
Reader can obtain the Schwarzschild orbit equation d^2u/dphi^2 + u = m/h^2 + 3mu^2 from the geodesic Lagrangian, including conserved k and h and the argument for planar motion.

Reader can carry out a first-order perturbation expansion of the relativistic Binet equation, identify the secular phi sin phi term, recombine it into a slowly rotating ellipse, and derive Delta phi = 6 pi G M / (c^2 a (1 - e^2)) per orbit.
Reader can explain why only about 43 arcseconds per century of Mercury's observed perihelion advance is anomalous, and evaluate the relativistic prediction numerically.
Reader can derive the light-deflection angle 4GM/(c^2 D) by perturbing a straight line u = sin(phi)/D and reading the deflection from the asymptote angles, and compute 1.75 arcsec for a grazing ray.
Reader can describe gravitational lensing qualitatively (convergence to a caustic, double images, achromaticity, sensitivity to dark mass).
Reader can set up the Shapiro radar delay integral, identify the flat-space and logarithmic terms, and estimate the excess delay for a ray grazing the Sun.

Reader can write the PPN-expanded static spherically symmetric metric, relate A_2 and B_1 to beta and gamma, and state how the perihelion, deflection and time-delay predictions scale with (2 + 2 gamma - beta)/3 and (1 + gamma)/2.

Reader can use the rubber-sheet model and the Schwarzschild spatial embedding diagram as intuition pumps while stating their limitations (space not space-time, half the light bending, no physical meaning off the surface).

teaching_approach.summary: A tests-driven closing chapter that alternates between a physical argument or experiment and an explicit calculation. It opens with the redshift because it needs only the equivalence principle, turns the experimental support for the equivalence principle into a justification for considering only metric theories, then treats orbits and light rays with a single reusable recipe: Lagrangian for Schwarzschild geodesics, conserved quantities, u = 1/r orbit equation, nondimensionalize, expand in a small epsilon, and read off the observable. Each derivation is immediately confronted with numbers and a short history. Only at the end are the results generalized to PPN parameters so the same tests discriminate among metric theories. It finishes with a deliberately qualitative rubber-sheet model whose limitations are spelled out.
narrative_arc: Frame the solar-system tests as weak-field checks and preview the PPN comparison and strong-field evidence (binary pulsars, LIGO) that lies beyond them.
Motivate gravitational redshift with a perpetual-motion paradox built from buckets of excited and ground-state atoms on a chain between Earth and Sun.

Make it quantitative in any static space-time by comparing proper-time and coordinate-time crest intervals for two static clocks, then take the weak-field and Schwarzschild limits and evaluate the solar value.
Survey redshift experiments: solar and white-dwarf spectra, Pound-Rebka with the Mossbauer effect, rocket and spacecraft clocks, and the GPS correction budget.
Present the Eotvos torsion balance and its successors as precision tests of the weak equivalence principle.
State the three-part Einstein equivalence principle, list its experimental support, and sketch why it forces a metric description of gravity (postulates of metric theories).
Review the Newtonian Kepler problem through Binet's equation and reduce the two-body problem to one body with reduced mass.

Repeat the analysis for Schwarzschild timelike geodesics with the variational method, obtain the relativistic Binet equation with its extra 3mu^2 term, and solve perturbatively to find the rotating ellipse and the perihelion advance; confront with Mercury, other planets, Icarus and a binary pulsar.

Reuse the recipe for null geodesics: straight line at zeroth order, first-order correction, deflection from the asymptote angles; confront with eclipse and radio data; introduce gravitational lensing.
Compute the round-trip radar travel time past the Sun, isolate the logarithmic excess delay, and compare with Venus radar and Viking data.
Generalize the metric with post-Newtonian coefficients, identify beta and gamma, restate the three tests with PPN factors, and quote the measured values.
Summarize the history in a chronology, then close Part C with the rubber-sheet model and embedding diagrams, including explicit caveats and a glimpse of gravitational waves as ripples.
signature_moves: Uses a perpetual-motion paradox, rather than an elevator, to force the existence of gravitational redshift from energy conservation.

Derives the redshift for any static metric using only the staticity argument that crest intervals in world time cannot pile up between the observers; stresses that the field equations were never used.
Runs a Newtonian derivation in full first (Binet's equation) so the relativistic orbit equation reads as 'the same equation plus one term', making the comparison line by line.
Systematic nondimensionalization before perturbing: defines u-tilde of order one and a small epsilon (3m^2/h^2 for orbits, 3m/D for light) so the ordering of terms is explicit.
Rewrites the growing secular term e epsilon phi sin phi as a phase shift cos[phi(1 - epsilon)], turning a formal correction into the picture of a rotating ellipse.
Extracts the light deflection from the two asymptote angles at which u vanishes instead of integrating a trajectory.
Reframes the tests retrospectively as measurements of PPN parameters, so experiments first used to favour Einstein over Newton become constraints on all metric theories.
Ends with a physical tabletop model (rubber sheet and marble) and explicitly lists what it gets wrong.
Routinely marks steps '(exercise)', '(check)' or '(why?)' and pushes the algebra into keyed exercises.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Positions the solar-system tests as probes of the weak-field regime where GR differs only slightly from Newton, announces the PPN framework as the tool for comparing GR with rival theories, and notes that strong-field predictions (early universe, black holes, gravitational waves) need other evidence such as binary-pulsar orbital decay and the 2015 LIGO detection. Recalls the three original classical tests plus radar delay, and explains that redshift really tests the equivalence principle; combined with tests of local Lorentz and position invariance it supports the Einstein equivalence principle and hence metric theories. It adds that the PPN comparison forces the solar-system predictions of the twenty-odd rival relativistic theories proposed since 1915 to lie very close to GR's, and promises a closing chronology.
key_moves: Distinguish weak-field (perturbatively Newtonian) tests from strong-field phenomena.
Reclassify gravitational redshift as an equivalence-principle test rather than a test of the Schwarzschild solution.
Chain: redshift + Lorentz-invariance + position-invariance tests -> Einstein equivalence principle -> metric theory -> PPN comparison using the remaining tests.

sections.title: Gravitational red shift
sections.summary: A bucket chain carrying excited atoms down toward the Sun and ground-state atoms up, with emitted radiation mirrored back to Earth, would run forever unless light loses energy as it climbs; hence a redshift. For two static clocks in a static space-time, proper-time intervals between received crests relate through g_00 because the world-time interval between crests is the same at both ends, giving nu_2/nu_1 = sqrt(g_00(x_1)/g_00(x_2)) and, in the weak field, Delta nu/nu = (phi_1 - phi_2)/c^2, with no field equations used. The solar value is about -2.12 x 10^-6, but solar and white-dwarf observations are hard to interpret. Terrestrial and space tests follow: Pound-Rebka (22 m tower, Mossbauer gamma rays, Doppler compensation, agreement to about 1%), rocket and satellite clocks, Voyager at Saturn, and the 1976 maser clock on a Scout rocket. The section ends with GPS, where special-relativistic time dilation and gravitational frequency shift must both be corrected.
concepts: Gravity Probe A rocket redshift test
key_moves: Perpetual-motion paradox resolved only if radiation is degraded while climbing.
Proper time d tau^2 = g_00 (dx^0)^2 for each static clock, (16.1)-(16.2).
Staticity implies equal coordinate intervals dx_1^0 = dx_2^0 (16.3), else crests accumulate.
Ratio gives k and nu_2 = nu_1/k (16.4)-(16.5); redshift if g_00 is smaller at the emitter (16.6).
Weak-field substitution g_00 = 1 + 2 phi/c^2 yields (16.8); Schwarzschild potential yields (16.9)-(16.11).
Experimental narrative from astronomical to Mossbauer to clocks in space; GPS order-of-magnitude budget (16.12).

sections.title: The Eötvös experiment
sections.summary: Describes the torsion balance: two bodies of different composition on a horizontal rod hung from a fibre. Any composition-dependent difference in gravitational acceleration produces a torque proportional to the Eotvos ratio eta; rotating the apparatus, or letting the Earth's rotation do so when the Sun supplies g, modulates the torque so it can be separated from constant effects. Eotvos reached |eta| < 5 x 10^-9, Dicke's Princeton group 10^-11 (with the Sun as source and force feedback), Braginsky's Moscow group 10^-12 (from torsional motion), later confirmed by Su et al. (1994). The book presents the torsion balance as descended from the earlier pendulum tests of Newton and Bessel.
key_moves: Translate unequal accelerations of different materials into a torque on the suspension, (16.13).
Use a known modulation (turntable or Earth rotation relative to the Sun) to isolate the signal.
Track the historical improvement of the bound over three orders of magnitude.

sections.title: The Einstein equivalence principle
sections.summary: Introduces the Einstein equivalence principle as intermediate between the weak and strong versions of Chapter 9: universality of free fall, independence of local non-gravitational experiments from the velocity of the freely falling frame, and independence from place and time. Supporting evidence is listed (redshift and Eotvos tests; Michelson-Morley-type and source-velocity tests of light speed; clocks in rockets and satellites; spectral lines from distant galaxies; comparison with pulsar PSR 1937+21). Following Will, it argues that these requirements essentially leave special-relativistic local physics plus locally straight free-fall paths, i.e. geodesics of a Lorentzian metric, and states the three postulates of metric theories.
key_moves: Split the principle into three separately testable clauses and match each to experiments.
Heuristic argument: local velocity and position independence force special-relativistic local laws; locally unaccelerated test bodies become geodesics of a metric.
Conclude with metric-theory postulates, which licence the PPN comparison of §16.9.

sections.title: Classical Kepler motion
sections.summary: Reviews the Newtonian one-body problem: conservation of angular momentum confines the motion to a plane; in polar coordinates the equation of motion splits into R^2 phi-dot = h and a radial equation; the substitution u = 1/R converts time derivatives into phi derivatives, giving Binet's linear equation u'' + u = mu/h^2 whose solution is a conic l/R = 1 + e cos(phi - phi_0). The two-body problem reduces to this with reduced mass m_1 m_2/(m_1 + m_2) and mu = G(m_1 + m_2).
concepts: Conservation of angular momentum in central-force motion
Reduced mass and the two-body problem
key_moves: dL/dt = 0 for a central force, so the orbit is planar (16.16)-(16.17).
Polar components give R^2 phi-dot = h (16.19) and the radial equation (16.20).
Chain rule with phi-dot = h u^2 turns R-dot into -h du/dphi and R-double-dot into -h^2 u^2 u'' (16.22).
Binet's equation (16.23) and its conic solution (16.25) with l = h^2/mu, e = C h^2/mu.
Relative coordinate and Newton's third law reduce two bodies to one (16.27)-(16.29).

sections.title: Advance of the perihelion of Mercury
sections.summary: Treats a test particle on a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic using the Lagrangian 2K = 1. The t, theta and phi Euler-Lagrange equations plus the first integral suffice; spherical symmetry and the theta equation confine the motion to the equatorial plane; the t and phi equations give constants k and h. Substituting and using u = 1/r yields a first-order orbit equation and, on differentiating, the relativistic Binet equation with an extra 3mu^2 term. After nondimensionalizing with epsilon = 3m^2/h^2 (about 10^-7 for Mercury) a first-order perturbation expansion produces a secular e phi sin phi term, which recombines into an ellipse whose perihelion advances by 2 pi epsilon per orbit, i.e. 6 pi GM/(c^2 a (1 - e^2)). Observational context: Newtonian planetary perturbations, the 43 arcsec per century residual for Mercury, the Vulcan episode, the GR value 42.98, Table 16.1 for Venus, Earth and Icarus, and the 4.2 degrees per year periastron advance of PSR 1913+16.
concepts: Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass
key_moves: Lagrangian (16.30) with 2K = 1 for proper-time parametrization; use a = 0, 2, 3 equations (16.31)-(16.33) plus the first integral.
Choose theta(0) = pi/2, theta-dot(0) = 0; the theta equation forces all higher theta derivatives to vanish, so motion is equatorial.
Integrate to r^2 phi-dot = h (16.34) and (1 - 2m/r) t-dot = k (16.35); substitute into (16.30) to get (16.36), then (16.37) and (16.38).
Size the new term: its ratio to the Newtonian term is 3h^2/r^2, small for planets.
Nondimensionalize u-tilde = h^2 u/m, epsilon = 3m^2/h^2 (16.39)-(16.40); expand (16.41)-(16.43); solve with trial form (16.44)-(16.45).
Keep the growing term and recombine: u = (m/h^2){1 + e cos[phi(1 - epsilon)]} (16.47); radial period in phi is 2 pi (1 + epsilon).
Use h^2 = m a (1 - e^2) to get (16.49); eliminate M with Kepler's third law to get (16.50).
Confront with Mercury's residual 43 arcsec/century and Table 16.1.

sections.title: Bending of light
sections.summary: Repeats the orbit analysis for null geodesics (right-hand side of the Lagrangian zero, affine parameter), giving u'' + u = 3mu^2. With m = 0 the solution u = sin(phi - phi_0)/D is a straight line with closest approach D. With epsilon = 3m/D (order 10^-6 at the solar limb) a first-order correction (1 + C cos phi + cos^2 phi)/3 is found; requiring u = 0 at the two asymptotic angles gives small angles epsilon_1 and epsilon_2 whose sum is the deflection 4m/D = 4GM/(c^2 D), 1.75 arcsec for a grazing ray. Then: eclipse star-field comparisons, Eddington's 1919 expedition and its shaky accuracy, results spread from 0.7 to 1.55 times the prediction, the 2017 eclipse, radio interferometry of quasars, and gravitational lensing (caustics, double images, the 1980 twin quasar 0957+561, Hubble images, achromaticity, lensing as a probe of invisible mass).
key_moves: Null version of the orbit equation (16.51); flat limit (16.52) with straight-line solution (16.53).
Nondimensionalize with u-tilde = D u and epsilon = 3m/D (16.54)-(16.55); expand (16.56)-(16.57).
First-order trajectory (16.58) with an arbitrary constant C for asymmetry of orientation.
Set u = 0 at phi = -epsilon_1 and phi = pi + epsilon_2 using small-angle approximations; C cancels on adding, giving (16.59)-(16.60).
Observational narrative: eclipse photography, VLBI, lensing geometry (Figs. 16.11-16.14).

sections.title: Time delay of light
sections.summary: Shapiro's fourth test: radar signals passing near the Sun take longer than flat-space geometry suggests. From the null Lagrangian in the equatorial plane with constants h and k, the closest-approach condition r-dot = 0 at r = D fixes h^2/k^2, which lets phi be eliminated to give (dr/dt)^2 as a function of r. Expanding dt/dr to first order in m and integrating from D to the planet's and Earth's orbital radii yields a flat-space term, a logarithmic term and a small correction; the round trip excess for a ray grazing the Sun is about 4m[ln(4 D_P D_E / D_S^2) + 1]. Venus radar echoes (about 200 microseconds, 5%) and the 1976 Viking Mars data (better than 1%) confirm it.
concepts: Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass
key_moves: Null Lagrangian (16.61) with conserved h and k (16.62)-(16.63).
Turning point r-dot = 0 at r = D gives h^2/k^2 = D^2/(1 - 2m/D) (16.65).
Eliminate phi via (dphi/dt)^2 (16.66) to get (dr/dt)^2 (16.67) and dt in terms of dr (16.68).
Expand in m to (16.69); integrate the three terms (16.70)-(16.71), with the substitution r = D cosh u suggested for two of them.
Double the sum of the two legs for the round trip (16.72)-(16.73); identify m = 0 limit as flat-space time.
Approximate for D near the solar radius to get the excess delay (16.74)-(16.75).

sections.title: The PPN parameters
sections.summary: Recounts how Eddington (1922 eclipse) introduced a parameter gamma and Robertson and Schiff added beta measuring non-linearity, and mentions Brans-Dicke theory (a variable G, coupling omega, GR as omega -> infinity) as a motivating alternative. Restricting to metric theories because of the Einstein equivalence principle (allowing at most very weak or short-range non-metric couplings, such as string theory might supply), it notes there are ten PPN parameters, eight of which concern momentum non-conservation or preferred frames/locations and are tightly bounded, leaving beta and gamma for the classical tests. The static spherically symmetric metric is written with dimensionless radius c^2 r/GM; A is expanded to second order and B to first, with A_2 = 2(beta - gamma) and B_1 = 2 gamma related to the isotropic-coordinate PPN form. The perihelion shift scales by (2 + 2 gamma - beta)/3, and the deflection and radar delay by (1 + gamma)/2. Quoted results: gamma = 1.000 +/- 0.002 (time delay), beta = 1.000 +/- 0.003 (Mercury), with solar oblateness shown to be too small to matter. Following Will, beta is glossed as a measure of the non-linearity of gravity and gamma as the curvature produced per unit rest mass; the three PPN-modified results are stated as obtainable by repeating the chapter's perturbation methods (exercise).
key_moves: Historical motivation: parametrizing the metric to quantify eclipse results.
Restrict to metric theories on the strength of the Einstein equivalence principle; discard the eight non-classical PPN parameters.
Dimensional argument: M, G, c allow only one dimensionless radius (16.77).
Newtonian limit fixes the 1/r-tilde term of A; B tends to 1; expand to next order.
Match to the isotropic PPN form (16.79) to identify A_2 and B_1 (Exercise 16.18).
Restate the three tests with PPN factors (16.80)-(16.82) and extract measured gamma then beta.

sections.title: A chronology of experimental and observational events
sections.summary: A dated list running from the 1919 eclipse expedition through Eotvos experiments, repeated eclipse campaigns, white-dwarf redshift, Pound-Rebka, Hughes-Drever, the CMB, pulsars, radar delay, the first black-hole candidate Cygnus X-1, the binary pulsar and its orbital decay, rocket redshift tests, the first gravitational lens, the double pulsar, Gravity Probe B, LIGO, and the Event Horizon Telescope image.
key_moves: Place the classical tests on a timeline that extends into strong-field and cosmological evidence.

sections.title: Rubber-sheet geometry
sections.summary: Closes the chapter and Part C with a tabletop model: a marble rolls straight on a flat taut sheet (special relativity) but orbits, and its elliptical path precesses, when a weight dents the sheet. The model is tied to the embedding of the Schwarzschild t = const, theta = pi/2 slice, ds^2 = (1 - 2m/r)^-1 dr^2 + r^2 dphi^2, in Euclidean 3-space, first for the vacuum solution and then with a stellar interior filling r < r_0, and used to picture light bending. Caveats: only the 2-surface has meaning; the picture shows curved space rather than space-time, so it gives only half the light deflection. It ends with Wheeler's slogan, the contrast with Newtonian action at a distance, and the idea that changes in the source propagate as ripples at the speed of light.
concepts: Finite propagation speed of gravitational influence
key_moves: Flat sheet = straight geodesics; dented sheet = orbits as straightest paths on a curved surface.
Replace the loose analogy by a precise object: an embedding of the spatial Schwarzschild geometry (16.83).
Interior solution caps the funnel (Fig. 16.19); rays across the dent picture deflection (Fig. 16.20).
Flag the factor-of-two shortfall and the meaninglessness of the embedding space.
Local, propagating influence replaces instantaneous action at a distance, pointing to gravitational waves.

sections.title: Exercises and further reading
sections.summary: Nineteen exercises keyed to sections fill in the redshift limit, Kepler's laws and energy, the two-body centre-of-mass problem, the Schwarzschild Euler-Lagrange and orbit equations, the perturbative solutions, the effective potential and ISCO, the photon sphere, the Shapiro integrals, and the PPN coefficient matching. Further reading recommends Hartle for tests and lensing, Will's book and Living Review for a complete treatment, Perlick's review on lensing, and sources for Wheeler's slogan.
key_moves: Push algebraic verification and extensions (ISCO at r = 6m, photon orbit at r = 3m) into exercises.

concepts.name: Classical tests of general relativity
concepts.definition: The historically first observational checks of GR, all in the Sun's weak field: perihelion advance of Mercury, deflection of starlight, gravitational redshift, and (added in 1964) the radar echo time delay.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed in the introduction as the organizing theme; each gets its own derivation and data section, and §16.9 reinterprets them as measurements of PPN parameters.
concepts.notes: The book notes redshift is really an equivalence-principle test, so only three of the four discriminate among metric theories.

concepts.name: Weak-field regime
concepts.definition: Situations where gravitational potentials satisfy |phi|/c^2 << 1 and speeds are small compared with c, so GR predictions are Newtonian plus small corrections that can be expanded in GM/(c^2 r).
concepts.how_introduced: Stated at the outset to limit what solar-system tests can establish, contrasted with strong-field phenomena such as black holes and gravitational waves from mergers.

concepts.name: Gravitational redshift
concepts.definition: The decrease in frequency measured by a static receiver higher in a gravitational potential for light emitted by an identical static source lower down; equivalently, clocks lower in a potential run slow relative to higher ones.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by a perpetual-motion paradox with atoms on a bucket chain, then derived for static observers in any static metric by comparing proper and coordinate time between successive crests.
concepts.notes: Any theory obeying the equivalence principle predicts it; the field equations are not needed.

concepts.name: Static space-time
concepts.definition: A space-time admitting coordinates (x^0, x^alpha) in which the metric components are independent of the world time x^0 and there are no time-space cross terms, so time translation is a symmetry and signals repeat identically when shifted in x^0.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the assumption that makes crest intervals in world time equal at emitter and receiver: otherwise crests would accumulate or drain between them.
concepts.notes: Formal definition was given in DIV ch15 §15.3; here only the time-independence of g_ab is used.

concepts.name: Fractional frequency shift
concepts.definition: The dimensionless ratio (nu_received - nu_emitted)/nu_emitted, negative for a redshift.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined right after the exact redshift ratio so the weak-field approximation can be stated as a difference of potentials.

concepts.name: Weak-field limit of the metric
concepts.definition: In a nearly Newtonian static field the time-time metric component is g_00 = 1 + 2 phi/c^2, where phi is the Newtonian potential; this identification underlies both the redshift formula and the leading PPN term.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 10 to reduce the exact redshift result to potential differences; reused in §16.9 to fix the first coefficient of A(r).

concepts.name: Mossbauer effect
concepts.definition: Recoil-free emission and resonant absorption of gamma rays by nuclei bound in a crystal lattice, producing lines so narrow (about one part in 10^12 or better) that tiny frequency shifts become measurable.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the technical breakthrough (1958) that made a terrestrial redshift test over tens of metres feasible.

concepts.name: Pound-Rebka experiment
concepts.definition: A 1960 terrestrial measurement of the gravitational frequency shift of Mossbauer gamma rays sent up a vertical tower of about 22 m (the Jefferson Physical Laboratory tower at Harvard), in which a small upward velocity of the source supplied a Doppler shift that restored resonant absorption.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the first precise terrestrial redshift test after astronomical tests proved ambiguous.
concepts.notes: The book quotes 0.997 +/- 0.009 of a predicted 4.92e-15, which is twice gh/c^2 for the tower, i.e. the difference between upward and downward runs. The iron-57 14.4 keV line and the 22.5 m height are standard background, not given in the book.

concepts.name: Gravity Probe A rocket redshift test
concepts.definition: A 1976 suborbital flight of a hydrogen-maser clock to about 10,000 km altitude, compared with a ground maser, that confirmed the gravitational frequency shift to a few parts in 10^4.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited as improving the Pound-Rebka accuracy by about two orders of magnitude; the text does not use the name Gravity Probe A.

concepts.name: Relativistic corrections in GPS
concepts.definition: Satellite navigation must correct satellite clock rates for special-relativistic time dilation (satellite clocks slow) and gravitational frequency shift (satellite clocks higher in the potential run fast relative to ground clocks); uncorrected, the net rate offset of about 38 microseconds per day would accumulate to kilometre-scale position errors.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as a modern, everyday application at the end of the redshift section with an order-of-magnitude comparison of the two effects.
concepts.notes: Treated as an application of gravitational redshift and time dilation. See gaps: the printed GPS numbers and the claim that both effects act in the same direction need correction.

concepts.name: Eotvos experiment
concepts.definition: A torsion-balance test of universality of free fall: two different materials on a rod suspended by a thin fibre feel a net torque if their gravitational-to-inertial mass ratios differ; the torque is modulated by rotating the apparatus or by the Earth's rotation relative to the Sun.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced briefly because the equivalence principle is central; historical improvement from Eotvos to Dicke to Braginsky is narrated.

concepts.name: Eotvos ratio
concepts.definition: The dimensionless fractional difference in free-fall acceleration of two bodies, eta = 2|a_1 - a_2|/|a_1 + a_2|, which vanishes if the weak equivalence principle holds.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined through the torque formula and quoted as successive experimental bounds.
concepts.notes: The book calls eta 'a limit on the difference in acceleration'; the explicit ratio definition is standard (Will), not printed here.

concepts.name: Weak equivalence principle
concepts.definition: The trajectory of an uncharged test body in free fall depends only on its initial position and velocity, not on its internal structure or composition.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited as clause 1 of the Einstein equivalence principle; supported by Eotvos-type experiments and, in the book's framing, by redshift measurements.
concepts.notes: In DIV ch9 the labels 'weak' and 'strong' were used differently; this chapter follows the modern (Will) usage.

concepts.name: Local Lorentz invariance
concepts.definition: Results of small-scale experiments that do not involve gravity come out the same whatever the velocity of the freely falling laboratory carrying them out; local physics is Lorentz invariant.
concepts.how_introduced: Clause 2 of the Einstein equivalence principle, supported by refined Michelson-Morley tests, independence of light speed from source velocity (binary X-ray sources, pion decays) and isotropy of light speed.

concepts.name: Local position invariance
concepts.definition: Results of small-scale experiments that do not involve gravity do not depend on the location or epoch at which the freely falling laboratory performs them, so dimensionless constants are the same everywhere and always.
concepts.how_introduced: Clause 3 of the Einstein equivalence principle, supported by rocket and satellite clocks (space) and by distant-galaxy spectral lines and pulsar timing comparisons (time).

concepts.name: Einstein equivalence principle
concepts.definition: The conjunction of the weak equivalence principle, local Lorentz invariance and local position invariance; it implies that gravity can be described by a metric whose geodesics are free-fall paths and in whose local inertial frames non-gravitational physics is special-relativistic.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a version between the weak and strong principles of Chapter 9 that is directly supported by experiment, followed by a plausibility argument (after Will) that it forces a metric theory.

concepts.name: Metric theories of gravity
concepts.definition: Theories in which (1) space-time has a symmetric metric, (2) freely falling test bodies follow its geodesics, and (3) non-gravitational laws in local freely falling frames take their special-relativistic form; GR and Brans-Dicke theory are examples.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained as a consequence of the Einstein equivalence principle and used to restrict the class of rivals compared through PPN parameters.

concepts.name: Kepler problem
concepts.definition: Motion of a test particle under an inverse-square central attraction F = -m mu r-hat / r^2; bound orbits are ellipses with the centre of force at a focus.
concepts.how_introduced: Reviewed as the Newtonian baseline so the relativistic orbit equation can be compared term by term.

concepts.name: Conservation of angular momentum in central-force motion
aliases: h as angular momentum per unit mass
concepts.definition: For a central force the angular momentum L = r x m r-dot is constant, so motion lies in a fixed plane and R^2 phi-dot = h is constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by differentiating L and noting both cross products vanish; recovered again in the relativistic case from the phi Euler-Lagrange equation.

concepts.name: Binet equation
concepts.definition: The orbit equation for central-force motion written for u(phi) = 1/R(phi); for an inverse-square force it is linear, u'' + u = mu/h^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by the chain rule with phi-dot = h u^2 converting time derivatives of R to phi derivatives of u.
prerequisites: Conservation of angular momentum in central-force motion

concepts.name: Conic section orbit
concepts.definition: The solution l/R = 1 + e cos(phi - phi_0), where the semi-latus rectum l = h^2/mu sets size, eccentricity e sets shape (ellipse for 0 < e < 1), and phi_0 sets orientation of the perihelion, the point of closest approach.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the general solution of Binet's equation.

concepts.name: Reduced mass and the two-body problem
concepts.definition: Two point masses in mutual Newtonian attraction have a relative coordinate r = r_1 - r_2 obeying a one-body inverse-square equation with reduced mass m_1 m_2/(m_1 + m_2) and mu = G(m_1 + m_2).
concepts.how_introduced: Shown by subtracting the two equations of motion using Newton's third law.
concepts.notes: Symbol m is reused in §16.6 for GM/c^2, a different quantity.

concepts.name: Variational method for geodesics
concepts.definition: Geodesics extremize the integral of K = (1/2) g_ab x-dot^a x-dot^b; the Euler-Lagrange equations reproduce the geodesic equations, and K itself is constant (1/2 for proper-time parametrization, 0 for null curves).
concepts.how_introduced: Chosen as the simplest route to Schwarzschild geodesics; only the three simplest Euler-Lagrange equations plus the first integral are used.

concepts.name: Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass
concepts.definition: Because the Schwarzschild Lagrangian does not depend on t or phi, (1 - 2m/r) t-dot = k and r^2 phi-dot = h are constant along geodesics; for timelike motion k is energy per unit rest mass (in units of c^2) and h angular momentum per unit mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by direct integration of the t and phi Euler-Lagrange equations and compared with Newtonian angular momentum.
concepts.notes: The book does not interpret k physically; the energy interpretation is standard.

concepts.name: Equatorial-plane confinement of Schwarzschild geodesics
concepts.definition: By spherical symmetry one may choose theta(0) = pi/2 and theta-dot(0) = 0; the theta equation then gives theta-double-dot(0) = 0 and all higher derivatives vanish, so the geodesic stays in the equatorial plane.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as a question: does the Newtonian planarity survive in GR? Answered with the theta Euler-Lagrange equation and a '(why?)' prompt.
concepts.notes: A cleaner justification is uniqueness of ODE solutions: theta = pi/2 is itself a solution with the same initial data.

concepts.name: Relativistic Binet equation
concepts.definition: For timelike Schwarzschild geodesics, u = 1/r satisfies u'' + u = m/h^2 + 3mu^2; the last term, absent in Newtonian theory, is smaller than the Newtonian one by 3h^2/r^2 (about 3v^2/c^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by substituting h and k into the first integral, using u = 1/r, and differentiating the resulting first-order equation.
prerequisites: Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass

concepts.name: Regular perturbation expansion
concepts.definition: Writing the solution of an equation containing a small dimensionless parameter epsilon as u_0 + epsilon u_1 + O(epsilon^2) and solving order by order, after nondimensionalizing so that u_0 is of order one.
concepts.how_introduced: Used twice in parallel (orbits with epsilon = 3m^2/h^2, light with epsilon = 3m/D) after an explicit nondimensionalization step.

concepts.name: Secular term
concepts.definition: A term in a perturbative solution that grows without bound with the independent variable (here e phi sin phi), arising from forcing at the natural frequency; it signals a slow cumulative change such as a frequency or orientation shift.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified as the most important first-order correction because it grows each revolution, then resummed into cos[phi(1 - epsilon)].
concepts.notes: The naive expansion is only valid while epsilon phi << 1; the resummed form is a two-timing/Poincare-Lindstedt result.

concepts.name: Perihelion precession
concepts.definition: The slow rotation of the major axis of a bound orbit in its plane; in Schwarzschild the perihelion advances by 6 pi GM/(c^2 a (1 - e^2)) radians per orbit.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from the perturbed orbit u = (m/h^2){1 + e cos[phi(1 - epsilon)]}: successive perihelia are 2 pi (1 + epsilon) apart in phi.

concepts.name: Anomalous perihelion advance of Mercury
concepts.definition: The part of Mercury's observed perihelion advance (about 43 arcsec per century out of roughly 5600 in Earth-based coordinates, most due to precession of the equinoxes and planetary perturbations) that Newtonian perturbation theory could not explain, and which GR accounts for.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented after the derivation with the Newtonian n-body background, the failed Vulcan hypothesis, and the GR value 42.98.
concepts.notes: The total observed figure (~5600 arcsec/century) is standard background, not stated in the book.

concepts.name: Null geodesic
concepts.definition: A geodesic with zero tangent length, g_ab x-dot^a x-dot^b = 0, parametrized by an affine parameter rather than proper time; light rays in vacuum follow null geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Brought in by setting the right-hand side of the Lagrangian first integral to zero and reinterpreting the dot.

concepts.name: Gravitational deflection of light
concepts.definition: A light ray passing a mass M with closest approach D is turned through 4GM/(c^2 D) radians (1.75 arcsec at the solar limb), making background stars appear displaced away from the mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by perturbing the straight line u = sin(phi)/D and finding the two asymptotic directions where u = 0.
concepts.notes: Half of the GR value comes from the time part of the metric (the '1' in (1+gamma)/2) and half from spatial curvature (gamma).

concepts.name: Impact parameter
concepts.definition: For the unperturbed straight ray, the perpendicular distance D from the centre to the line; to first order it is also the closest-approach coordinate radius used in the deflection and delay formulae.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the constant in u = sin(phi - phi_0)/D, interpreted via Fig. 16.9, and reused as the turning-point radius in §16.8.
concepts.notes: Strictly the impact parameter b = h/k and the closest approach radius differ at order m; the book uses D for both roles in different sections.

concepts.name: Eclipse measurement of light deflection
concepts.definition: Comparison of photographs of a star field taken during a total solar eclipse with photographs of the same field taken when the Sun is elsewhere, revealing outward radial displacement of stars near the solar limb.
concepts.how_introduced: Described with Fig. 16.11 and the 1919 story, followed by a candid account of large systematic errors and scattered results.

concepts.name: Radio interferometric light-deflection measurement
concepts.definition: Measurement of the change in apparent angular separation of compact radio sources (quasars) as the Sun passes near them, using very long baseline interferometry; avoids eclipses and optical systematics.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the modern, precise replacement for eclipse photography (Lebach et al. 1995).

concepts.name: Gravitational lens
concepts.definition: A mass distribution that deflects light from background sources, focusing parallel rays toward a caustic and producing multiple, displaced or distorted images; the deflection is independent of frequency and depends only on mass, visible or not.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by drawing families of parallel rays bent by the Sun and a schematic double image, then the 1980 double quasar and Hubble images.
concepts.notes: Contrast with glass lenses: point-mass lens has no single focus; deflection falls off as 1/D so rays nearer the mass cross closer.

concepts.name: Shapiro time delay
concepts.definition: The extra coordinate travel time of a light signal passing through a gravitational field; for a radar round trip Earth-planet-Earth grazing the Sun it is about 4GM/c^3 [ln(4 D_P D_E / D_S^2) + 1].
concepts.how_introduced: Proposed by Shapiro in 1964; derived by eliminating phi from the null Lagrangian, expanding dt/dr to first order in m and integrating each leg.
prerequisites: Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass
concepts.notes: Observed as the time variation of echo delays as the planet approaches superior conjunction; the 'flat-space' comparison is coordinate dependent.

concepts.name: Parametrized post-Newtonian formalism
concepts.definition: A scheme that writes the weak-field, slow-motion metric of any metric theory as the Newtonian metric plus post-Newtonian terms with ten theory-dependent coefficients, so that experiments measure the coefficients and theories are compared through them.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated historically (Eddington, Robertson, Schiff) and by rival theories such as Brans-Dicke; restricted here to static spherical symmetry so only beta and gamma appear.

concepts.name: PPN parameter gamma
concepts.definition: The post-Newtonian coefficient measuring how much spatial curvature is produced per unit rest mass; it multiplies the 2GM/(c^2 rho) term in the spatial part of the isotropic metric and equals 1 in GR.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as Eddington's parameter for analysing the 1922 eclipse, then identified via B_1 = 2 gamma; controls deflection and delay through (1 + gamma)/2.
concepts.notes: Cassini (2003) gives gamma - 1 = (2.1 +/- 2.3) x 10^-5, much tighter than the book's value.

concepts.name: PPN parameter beta
concepts.definition: The post-Newtonian coefficient of the (GM/c^2 rho)^2 term in g_00, measuring how much non-linearity there is in the superposition law for gravity; equals 1 in GR.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the second parameter of Robertson and Schiff; identified via A_2 = 2(beta - gamma); measured from Mercury's perihelion once gamma is known.

concepts.name: General static spherically symmetric metric
concepts.definition: Any static spherically symmetric line element can be written ds^2 = A(r) c^2 dt^2 - B(r) dr^2 - r^2 (dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2) with r the areal radius.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken from Chapter 15 and expanded in inverse powers of the dimensionless radius c^2 r/GM to define post-Newtonian coefficients.

concepts.name: Isotropic coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates (t, rho, theta, phi) in which the spatial part of a spherically symmetric metric is conformally flat, proportional to d rho^2 + rho^2 (dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2); the standard PPN parameters are defined in this form.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to state the PPN metric (16.79); the relation to areal radius is left to Exercise 16.18 via r = rho + const + O(1/rho).

concepts.name: Brans-Dicke theory
concepts.definition: A 1961 scalar-tensor alternative to GR in which the effective gravitational constant is set by a dynamical scalar field, with a coupling constant omega; it approaches GR as omega -> infinity and predicts gamma = (1 + omega)/(2 + omega).
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the leading example of a theory motivated by Mach's principle that the PPN tests can constrain.
concepts.notes: The gamma formula is standard (Will), not given in the book.

concepts.name: Geometrized mass
concepts.definition: The mass parameter expressed as a length, m = GM/c^2 (about 1.48 km for the Sun), used with c = 1 so m, r and h all carry dimensions of length.
concepts.how_introduced: Used throughout the orbit and light derivations and converted back to non-relativistic units via (15.55) at the end of each.

concepts.name: Solar oblateness
concepts.definition: Flattening of the rotating Sun, which adds a Newtonian quadrupole contribution to planetary perihelion advance and could mimic or mask a relativistic effect.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as the caveat to the spherical-Sun assumption behind the beta bound; Brown et al. (1989) helioseismology shows it is too small to matter.

concepts.name: Binary pulsar periastron advance
concepts.definition: The relativistic rotation of the orbit of the Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar, about 4.2 degrees per year, which agrees with GR and helps fix the component masses.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned after Mercury as a strong-field-adjacent confirmation, with detailed treatment deferred to Chapter 21.

concepts.name: Effective potential for Schwarzschild orbits
concepts.definition: Radial motion of a timelike equatorial geodesic obeys (1/2) r-dot^2 + V(r) = k^2/2 with V(r) = (1/2)(1 - 2m/r)(1 + h^2/r^2), so turning points and circular orbits are read from V.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only in Exercise 16.12, as a bridge to Part D.
prerequisites: Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass

concepts.name: Innermost stable circular orbit
concepts.definition: The smallest radius at which stable circular timelike orbits exist in Schwarzschild, r = 6m, reached when h^2 = 12m^2 and the maximum and minimum of V(r) merge.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in Exercise 16.12 from the turning points of the effective potential.

concepts.name: Photon sphere
concepts.definition: The radius r = 3m in Schwarzschild at which light can move on an (unstable) circular orbit.
concepts.how_introduced: Set as Exercise 16.15 using the null orbit equation in the equatorial plane.

concepts.name: Rubber-sheet model
concepts.definition: A qualitative tabletop analogy in which a weight dents a taut rubber sheet and marbles rolling on it follow curved paths, standing in for geodesic motion in the curved geometry produced by a mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Closes Part C as an intuition aid, then made more precise with embedding diagrams and hedged with explicit limitations.
concepts.notes: The model relies on Earth's gravity to make marbles fall into the dent, so it presupposes the effect it illustrates.

concepts.name: Embedding diagram
concepts.definition: A picture of a 2D spatial slice (here t = const, theta = pi/2 of Schwarzschild, ds^2 = (1 - 2m/r)^-1 dr^2 + r^2 dphi^2) as a surface of revolution in Euclidean 3-space whose induced distances equal the slice's proper distances; only the surface, not the surrounding space, has meaning.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered to connect the rubber sheet with the actual geometry, for vacuum (Fig. 16.18), a star with interior (Fig. 16.19), and light bending (Fig. 16.20).
concepts.notes: The profile z(r) is standard (not printed in the book).

concepts.name: Finite propagation speed of gravitational influence
concepts.definition: In GR a change in a source alters the geometry locally and the change propagates outward at the speed of light, unlike Newtonian gravity where the field everywhere responds instantaneously.
concepts.how_introduced: Closing remark of the rubber-sheet section, as a first glimpse of gravitational waves (Part E).

key_equations.name: Proper time of emitter clock
key_equations.meaning: For a static clock only dx^0 is non-zero, so the proper-time interval between emitted crests is sqrt(g_00) times the world-time interval.
key_equations.symbols: tau proper time; x^0 world time; x_1^alpha fixed spatial position of emitter; g_00 time-time metric component

key_equations.name: Proper time of receiver clock
key_equations.meaning: The receiver records kd tau of its own proper time between the arrival of the same two crests.
key_equations.symbols: k ratio of received to emitted proper-time intervals

key_equations.name: Staticity condition
key_equations.meaning: In a static space-time every crest takes the same world time to travel between the fixed observers, so world-time intervals are equal at both ends.

key_equations.name: Redshift factor
key_equations.meaning: Ratio of proper-time intervals follows purely from g_00 at the two positions.

key_equations.name: Received frequency
key_equations.meaning: Exact frequency ratio between static emitter and static receiver in any static metric.
key_equations.symbols: nu_1 emitted (proper) frequency; nu_2 frequency measured by receiver

key_equations.meaning: Light from a place of smaller g_00 (deeper potential) arrives redshifted.

key_equations.name: Fractional frequency shift
key_equations.meaning: Definition of the observable shift.

key_equations.name: Weak-field g_00 (recalled from (10.49))
key_equations.meaning: Links metric to Newtonian potential in the weak-field limit.

key_equations.name: Weak-field redshift
key_equations.meaning: Fractional shift equals the potential difference (emitter minus receiver) over c^2; derived without field equations.
key_equations.symbols: phi_1, phi_2 potentials at emitter and receiver

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild weak-field redshift
key_equations.meaning: Using phi = -GM/r; the shift is negative (red) when the emitter is deeper.
key_equations.symbols: M central mass; r_1 emitter radius; r_2 receiver radius

key_equations.meaning: Upward-travelling light is redshifted.

key_equations.name: Solar surface redshift
key_equations.meaning: Evaluated for emission at the solar radius and reception at 1 AU, ignoring Earth's field.

key_equations.name: GPS gravitational term (as printed)
key_equations.meaning: Intended as the fractional gravitational frequency shift for a GPS orbit. As printed the number is about 100 times too large: GM_e/(c^2 R_S) is about 1.7e-10 for R_S = 2.66e4 km, and the relevant ground-to-orbit difference is about 5.3e-10.
key_equations.symbols: M_e Earth mass; R_S GPS orbital radius

key_equations.name: Eotvos torque
key_equations.meaning: Schematic size of the torque on the fibre if two materials fall with different accelerations; proportional to the Eotvos ratio and the rod length.
key_equations.symbols: eta Eotvos ratio; l rod length; g gravitational acceleration; k unit vector along fibre; i unit vector along rod

key_equations.name: Newtonian one-body equation
key_equations.meaning: Newton's second law for an inverse-square central force (16.14).

key_equations.name: Angular momentum conservation
key_equations.latex: \mathbf L=\mathbf r\times m\dot{\mathbf r},\qquad \frac{\mathrm d\mathbf L}{\mathrm dt}=0\Rightarrow\mathbf L=m\mathbf h
key_equations.meaning: Central forces exert no torque, so motion is confined to the plane perpendicular to h.
key_equations.symbols: h constant angular momentum per unit mass

key_equations.name: Equation of motion in plane polar coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Radial and transverse components of acceleration.
Transverse component integrated: constant areal rate.
Radial equation of motion.

key_equations.name: Chain rule with u = 1/R
key_equations.meaning: Converts time derivatives to phi derivatives using phi-dot = h u^2.
Second derivative from the same chain rule.

key_equations.name: Binet's equation
key_equations.meaning: Linear orbit equation for inverse-square attraction.

key_equations.name: Conic orbit
key_equations.meaning: General solution: a conic with focus at the centre of force.
key_equations.symbols: l semi-latus rectum; e eccentricity; phi_0 perihelion direction

key_equations.name: Two-body reduction
key_equations.meaning: Relative motion of two gravitating bodies is a one-body Kepler problem.
key_equations.symbols: r = r_1 - r_2; m reduced mass

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild timelike Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: First integral of the geodesic equations with proper-time parametrization.

key_equations.name: Euler-Lagrange equations for t, theta, phi
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\tau}[(1-2m/r)\dot t]=0,\quad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\tau}(r^2\dot\theta)-r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\phi^2=0,\quad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\tau}(r^2\sin^2\theta\,\dot\phi)=0
key_equations.meaning: Together with (16.30) these four equations determine t, r, theta, phi as functions of tau.

key_equations.name: Relativistic angular momentum
key_equations.meaning: Integral of the phi equation in the equatorial plane.
key_equations.symbols: h angular momentum per unit rest mass

key_equations.name: Energy constant
key_equations.meaning: Integral of the t equation.
key_equations.symbols: k conserved energy per unit rest mass

key_equations.meaning: First integral after eliminating t-dot.

key_equations.name: First-order orbit equation
key_equations.meaning: Exact equation for the orbit projected onto t = const; integrable with elliptic functions.

key_equations.name: Relativistic Binet equation
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian Binet equation plus a small relativistic term; the source of perihelion advance.

key_equations.name: Nondimensional orbit equation
key_equations.latex: \varepsilon=\frac{3m^2}{h^2},\qquad \frac{\mathrm d^2\tilde u}{\mathrm d\phi^2}+\tilde u=1+\varepsilon\tilde u^2,\quad\tilde u=\frac{h^2u}{m}
key_equations.meaning: Scaled so the Newtonian solution is of order one and the correction is multiplied by a small epsilon (about 1e-7 for Mercury).

key_equations.name: First-order perturbation equations
key_equations.latex: \tilde u=\tilde u_0+\varepsilon\tilde u_1+O(\varepsilon^2),\quad \tilde u_0''+\tilde u_0=1,\quad \tilde u_1''+\tilde u_1=\tilde u_0^2
key_equations.meaning: Order-by-order equations; the zeroth order is the Kepler conic u_0 = 1 + e cos phi.

key_equations.name: Particular solution
key_equations.meaning: Forcing (1 + e^2/2) + 2e cos phi + (e^2/2) cos 2phi; the cos phi part resonates and produces phi sin phi.
Solution to first order (called 'general' in the book, although homogeneous first-order terms are absorbed into e and phi_0).

key_equations.name: Precessing ellipse
key_equations.meaning: Keeping only the secular term and resumming it into a phase: an ellipse whose orientation rotates.
Angular period between successive perihelia.

key_equations.name: Perihelion advance per orbit
key_equations.meaning: Using h^2 = m a(1 - e^2) and m = GM/c^2; about 0.1 arcsec per orbit for Mercury.

key_equations.name: Perihelion advance from orbital elements
key_equations.meaning: Mass eliminated with Kepler's third law; favours short-period, eccentric orbits such as Mercury's.

key_equations.name: Null orbit equation
key_equations.meaning: Light-ray analogue of (16.38). With 0 instead of 1 on the right of the Lagrangian first integral, the constant (k^2 - 1)/h^2 becomes k^2/h^2 and the 2mu/h^2 term disappears, so after differentiating in phi only the relativistic 3mu^2 term survives on the right.

key_equations.name: Flat-space straight line
key_equations.meaning: With m = 0 the ray is a straight line whose perpendicular distance from the origin is D.

key_equations.name: Nondimensional light equation
key_equations.meaning: Small parameter about 6e-6 for a ray grazing the Sun (book: order 1e-6).

key_equations.latex: \tilde u=\tilde u_0+\varepsilon\tilde u_1,\quad\tilde u_0=\sin\phi,\quad\tilde u_1''+\tilde u_1=\sin^2\phi
key_equations.meaning: First-order equation forced by sin^2 phi; solution (1 + C cos phi + cos^2 phi)/3.

key_equations.name: Perturbed light ray
key_equations.meaning: Straight line plus a small bending correction.

key_equations.name: Asymptote conditions
key_equations.meaning: u = 0 at phi = -epsilon_1 and phi = pi + epsilon_2 with small-angle approximations.

key_equations.name: Light deflection
key_equations.meaning: Total deflection angle; 1.75 arcsec for a ray grazing the Sun.

key_equations.name: Null Lagrangian in equatorial plane
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for the radar delay.

key_equations.name: Turning-point constants
key_equations.meaning: Closest approach fixes the ratio of the conserved quantities.
Angular rate in coordinate time.

key_equations.name: Radial coordinate speed of light
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate radial speed of the ray; inverted and square-rooted to give dt in terms of dr.

key_equations.name: Expanded integrand
key_equations.meaning: Accurate to first order in m (errors of order m^2).

key_equations.name: One-leg travel time
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate time from closest approach out to radius D_P: flat term, logarithmic delay, small correction.

key_equations.name: Round-trip time
key_equations.meaning: Full first-order radar round trip; first bracket is the m = 0 (flat) value.

key_equations.name: Shapiro excess delay
key_equations.meaning: Excess round-trip delay for a ray grazing the Sun (D close to D_S); about 200-250 microseconds for Venus.

key_equations.name: Static spherically symmetric metric (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: General form with two free functions. The book prints B(r) dt^2 in the second term, a typo for B(r) dr^2.

key_equations.name: Dimensionless radius
key_equations.meaning: The only dimensionless combination of r with M, G, c.

key_equations.latex: \mathrm ds^2=A(\tilde r)c^2\mathrm dt^2-B(\tilde r)\mathrm dr^2-r^2(\mathrm d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\phi^2)
key_equations.meaning: Metric in non-relativistic units with coefficients depending on r-tilde.

key_equations.name: Post-Newtonian expansions and PPN identification
key_equations.latex: A(\tilde r)=1-\frac{2}{\tilde r}+\frac{A_2}{\tilde r^2}+O(\tilde r^{-3}),\quad B(\tilde r)=1+\frac{B_1}{\tilde r}+O(\tilde r^{-2}),\quad A_2=2(\beta-\gamma),\ B_1=2\gamma
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian limit fixes the first term of A; next-order coefficients encode beta and gamma (Exercise 16.18).

key_equations.name: PPN metric in isotropic coordinates (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Defines beta and gamma. Recovered from the page render (lost in the text export). As printed, the spatial factor reads (1 - 2 gamma GM/c^2 rho) and c^2 dt^2 is missing; the plus sign is required for Schwarzschild (gamma = 1) and for B_1 = 2 gamma.

key_equations.name: PPN perihelion advance
key_equations.meaning: Perihelion shift per orbit in a general metric theory; reduces to (16.49) for beta = gamma = 1. Recovered from page render.

key_equations.name: PPN light deflection
key_equations.meaning: Deflection depends only on gamma.

key_equations.name: PPN Shapiro delay (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Delay depends only on gamma. The book prints D_S rather than D_S^2 inside the logarithm, inconsistent with (16.75).

key_equations.name: Measured PPN parameters (as quoted)
key_equations.meaning: Gamma from time delay; beta from Mercury's perihelion using that gamma. Both are dated: Cassini (2003) gives gamma - 1 = (2.1 +/- 2.3) x 10^-5.

key_equations.name: Spatial Schwarzschild slice
key_equations.meaning: 2D geometry of t = const, theta = pi/2, embedded in Euclidean 3-space to make the rubber-sheet picture precise.

key_equations.name: Effective potential (Exercise 16.12)
key_equations.meaning: Radial energy equation; stable circular orbits at r_+, merging with r_- at h^2 = 12m^2, r = 6m (ISCO).

key_equations.name: Newtonian orbit parameters from energy (Exercise 16.5)
key_equations.meaning: Eccentricity expressed through energy and angular momentum.

figures.label: Fig. 16.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Could a chain of atom-carrying buckets between Earth and Sun run forever?
figures.visual_description: A tall closed loop of chain with small buckets hangs between a small arc labelled Earth at the top and a dotted dome labelled Sun at the bottom. Buckets on the left side, labelled excited state atoms, have little radiating tick marks; buckets on the right, labelled ground state atoms, do not. Curved arrows show the left side moving down and the right side moving up. A parabolic mirror sits at the bottom near the Sun, and a pair of dashed vertical lines runs up the middle from the mirror to Earth, representing the returned radiation beam.
figures.what_it_teaches: Energy conservation plus mass-energy equivalence demand that radiation climbing out of a gravitational well loses energy; otherwise the heavier excited side would drive perpetual motion.

redesign.idea: Animated energy ledger for the bucket machine: the chain turns, atoms de-excite at the bottom, a photon packet climbs to the top, and a bar chart tracks energy gained by falling versus energy needed to re-excite.
redesign.interaction: Toggle 'photon keeps its frequency' versus 'photon redshifts'; in the first case a perpetual-energy counter climbs without bound, in the second the ledger balances exactly. Slider for field strength shows the redshift scaling as g h / c^2.

figures.label: Fig. 16.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Successive wave crests emitted by one static observer and received by another.
figures.visual_description: A spacetime diagram with x^0 vertical and x^alpha horizontal. Two vertical lines at x_1^alpha (labelled world-line of emitter) and x_2^alpha (world-line of absorber). Two parallel slanted lines with arrowheads run from the emitter's line up and to the right to the absorber's line, representing two successive crests. Small double arrows mark the vertical separation dx_1^0 on the emitter line and dx_2^0 on the absorber line.
figures.what_it_teaches: In a static space-time the second signal is the first translated in world time, so the coordinate intervals at emission and reception are equal; frequencies differ only through sqrt(g_00).

redesign.idea: Crest-counting diagram with two clocks: signal world lines are copies shifted in world time, while tick marks along each vertical world line are spaced by proper time sqrt(g_00) dx^0.
redesign.interaction: Drag the emitter and receiver along a potential well; tick spacing on each world line updates with g_00, the translated signal lines stay parallel, and a readout shows nu_2/nu_1. A 'break staticity' toggle makes g_00 time dependent and the signal lines stop being parallel.

figures.label: Fig. 16.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Geometry for the redshift of light from atoms at the solar surface received at Earth.
figures.visual_description: A large hatched disc labelled Sun with centre O and a short radius labelled r_1, a straight line from O to a small hatched circle labelled Earth at distance r_2.
figures.what_it_teaches: Sets the two radii in (16.9) for evaluating the solar redshift of about 2 parts per million.

redesign.idea: Redshift calculator with selectable emitters (Sun, white dwarf, neutron star, GPS orbit, Harvard tower).
redesign.interaction: Choose emitter and receiver; the page shows the potential curve phi(r) with both points marked, the vertical gap (phi_1 - phi_2)/c^2 as the fractional shift, and a spectral line sliding red.

figures.caption_paraphrase: No caption: decorative margin grid.
figures.visual_description: A narrow vertical strip of empty square cells, two columns wide, of the sort printed in the book's margins as a note-taking grid. It carries no physics content.
figures.what_it_teaches: Nothing; page furniture exported as an image.

redesign.idea: None.
redesign.interaction: None.

figures.label: Fig. 16.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: The Eotvos torsion balance.
figures.visual_description: A fine vertical wire (labelled) hangs from a hatched ceiling. At its lower end it holds the midpoint of a slightly tilted rod carrying small spheres m_1 (left) and m_2 (right). From the point where the wire meets the rod, arrows show k upward along the wire, i along the rod toward m_2, g downward and slightly off the vertical, and a tilted axis labelled omega with a circular arrow indicating rotation of the apparatus.
figures.what_it_teaches: If two materials fall with different accelerations, g has a component that twists the rod about the wire; rotation at omega turns a static torque into an oscillating signal.

redesign.idea: 3D torsion balance with two material choices and a slowly rotating turntable (or Earth rotation with the Sun as source).
redesign.interaction: Set the Eotvos ratio eta from 0 to 10^-8 and rotate the apparatus; the rod's twist angle and a torque trace versus time show the modulation at the rotation period, with noise floor sliders showing why Dicke and Braginsky reached 10^-11 and 10^-12.

figures.label: Fig. 16.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: An elliptical Kepler orbit.
figures.visual_description: An ellipse tilted relative to a horizontal x-axis, with the focus O on the axis. A straight line through O along the major axis is labelled Perihelion at its end, making angle phi_0 with the x-axis. A particle m with an arrow moves along the ellipse at upper left. A short segment l from O perpendicular to the major axis reaches the ellipse, with a right-angle mark (the semi-latus rectum).
figures.what_it_teaches: Identifies the meaning of l, e and phi_0 in the polar conic equation and defines the perihelion.

redesign.idea: Polar conic explorer tied to Binet's equation.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for l, e and phi_0 redraw the orbit and highlight the semi-latus rectum and perihelion; a second panel plots u(phi) = (1 + e cos(phi - phi_0))/l as a sinusoid offset from zero, so the learner sees an ellipse as a shifted cosine in u.

figures.label: Fig. 16.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Position vectors in the two-body problem.
figures.visual_description: A triangle: origin O at left, arrow r_1 from O to m_1 at the top, arrow r_2 from O to m_2 at right, and arrow r from m_2 pointing to m_1 along the third side.
figures.what_it_teaches: Defines the relative position vector used to reduce two bodies to one.
concepts: Reduced mass and the two-body problem

redesign.idea: Two-body animation with a toggle between centre-of-mass frame and relative-coordinate frame.
redesign.interaction: Mass-ratio slider shows both bodies orbiting the centre of mass while the relative vector traces a single Kepler ellipse identical for all mass ratios with the same m_1 + m_2.

figures.label: Fig. 16.7(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Motion of a test particle in space-time.
figures.visual_description: A vertical arrow labelled t at left and, beside it, a curve spiralling upward like a stretched helix, with an arrowhead near the top: the world line of an orbiting particle.
figures.what_it_teaches: An orbit is a helix-like world line in space-time; the planar 'orbit' is its shadow.

redesign.idea: Combined 3D view of world line and projection (see Fig. 16.7(b)).
redesign.interaction: Rotate a 3D space-time with time vertical; drag a light source overhead to cast the helix onto a t = const plane, showing the precessing orbit as the shadow.

figures.label: Fig. 16.7(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The same motion projected onto a surface of constant t.
figures.visual_description: A parallelogram representing a plane labelled t = constant, with a loop drawn on it that closes almost into an ellipse and ends in an arrowhead.
figures.what_it_teaches: The orbit equation in u(phi) describes the projection, not the world line itself.

redesign.idea: Paired with Fig. 16.7(a): the projection panel accumulates the orbit as the helix rises.
redesign.interaction: Time scrubber moves a marker up the helix and simultaneously along the projected rosette.

figures.label: Fig. 16.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: The perihelion precesses.
figures.visual_description: Three overlapping ellipses labelled Orbit 1, Orbit 2 and Orbit 3 share a focus O near their left ends, each turned further anticlockwise. Straight lines from O run along the major axes to dots on the far end of Orbit 1 and Orbit 2, and the angle between these two axis lines is marked 2 pi epsilon. Arrowheads on the curves show the sense of motion.
figures.what_it_teaches: Each revolution the ellipse's axis turns by 2 pi epsilon, producing a rosette.

redesign.idea: Precessing-orbit integrator that compares the exact relativistic Binet solution, the first-order perturbation with the secular term, and the resummed rotating ellipse.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for m/h (exaggerated to make precession visible) and eccentricity; curves for Newtonian, exact GR and the naive epsilon e phi sin phi approximation diverge visibly after several orbits, showing why the resummation is needed. A readout converts to arcsec per century for real planets.

figures.label: Fig. 16.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: A light ray travelling in a straight line in special relativity.
figures.visual_description: A straight ray with an arrowhead climbs from lower left to upper right and crosses the x-axis to the left of the origin O. From O a perpendicular segment D meets the ray (right-angle mark), and a segment r runs from O to a point P on the ray. A short line through O drawn parallel to the ray makes the angle phi_0 with the x-axis, and the larger arc phi is the polar angle of OP measured from the x-axis.
figures.what_it_teaches: Geometric meaning of u = sin(phi - phi_0)/D: phi_0 is the direction of the line itself (where u = 0, i.e. r infinite) and D is its perpendicular distance from O.

redesign.idea: Straight-line polar plotter.
redesign.interaction: Drag the line; the plot of u(phi) = sin(phi - phi_0)/D updates, showing u vanishes at phi_0 and phi_0 + pi (the two ends of the line).

figures.label: Table 16.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Predicted and observed residual perihelion precessions.
figures.visual_description: A four-row table with columns Planet, GR prediction and Observed, in arcseconds per century: Mercury 43.0 vs 43.1 +/- 0.5; Venus 8.6 vs 8.4 +/- 4.8; Earth 3.8 vs 5.0 +/- 1.2; Icarus 10.3 vs 9.8 +/- 0.8. Printed in the margin beside the start of §16.7.
figures.what_it_teaches: Only Mercury and Icarus give sharp tests; other planets have small effects with large uncertainties.

redesign.idea: Error-bar chart of predicted versus observed precession for solar-system bodies.
redesign.interaction: Hover a body to see a, e and T; the predicted value recomputes from (16.50), and a toggle overlays modern ephemeris uncertainties.

figures.label: Fig. 16.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: A light ray is deflected by the Sun.
figures.visual_description: A horizontal baseline through a small hatched Sun. The solid curve labelled light ray leaves a true star at lower left, arches just above the Sun and reaches an eye at lower right. Two dashed straight asymptotes (labelled) cross above the Sun at an angle delta: one continues the ray's arriving direction backwards from the eye up to a star at upper left labelled apparent position of star; the other continues the ray's initial direction forwards to the upper right, where the ray's final segment is labelled apparent direction of light ray. The small angles epsilon_2 (left end) and epsilon_1 (right end) sit between each asymptote and the baseline; a radius r at polar angle phi joins the Sun to the ray.
figures.what_it_teaches: The deflection is the sum of the two asymptote angles, and the observer sees the star displaced outward along the arriving direction.

redesign.idea: Ray tracer around a point mass that integrates the null orbit equation and draws asymptotes.
redesign.interaction: Slide impact parameter D and mass; the ray, both asymptotes and angles epsilon_1, epsilon_2 update, with the sum compared against 4m/D and the exact value. Clicking 'Newtonian corpuscle' overlays the half-size deflection.

figures.label: Fig. 16.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: A star field (a) without the Sun and (b) during a total eclipse.
figures.visual_description: Two square panels side by side. (a) Six open star symbols scattered in an empty field. (b) A large hatched disc labelled Sun (obscured by Moon) with seven stars around its rim, each with a short arrow pointing radially outward to its displaced position.
figures.what_it_teaches: Deflection makes stars near the solar limb appear pushed away from the Sun; the effect is found by comparing plates taken months apart.

redesign.idea: Blink comparator for eclipse plates.
redesign.interaction: Toggle between night and eclipse plates; displacement vectors are exaggerated by a slider factor, scale as 1/distance from the Sun's centre, and the learner fits the 1.75 arcsec limb value with realistic measurement scatter (including 1919-style systematics).

figures.label: Fig. 16.12
figures.caption_paraphrase: The lensing action of a Schwarzschild field.
figures.visual_description: Two groups of three parallel rays with arrowheads enter from the left, one group above and one below a small hatched Sun. Each ray bends toward the axis, and they cross one another to the right of the Sun in a narrow region along the axis, with inner rays crossing closer than outer ones.
figures.what_it_teaches: A point mass focuses parallel light onto a caustic line rather than a single focal point, because rays nearer the mass are bent more.

redesign.idea: Bundle-of-rays lens simulator.
redesign.interaction: Adjust mass and bundle width; the crossing points of each ray pair on the axis are plotted, revealing a line caustic whose starting point moves with mass. A toggle compares with a glass lens with a single focus and colour dispersion.

figures.label: Fig. 16.13
figures.caption_paraphrase: How a gravitational lens makes a double image.
figures.visual_description: A star at upper left (labelled Image) sends two rays to an eye at right: an upper, nearly straight ray, and a lower ray that dips and bends sharply around a fuzzy galaxy before reaching the eye. A dashed line extends backward from the bent ray's final direction to a star at lower left labelled apparent image.
figures.what_it_teaches: Two paths around a lensing galaxy reach the observer from different directions, so one source appears twice.

redesign.idea: Source-lens-observer sandbox showing image positions.
redesign.interaction: Drag the source behind a galaxy lens; image positions solve the lens equation in real time, showing two images, merging into an Einstein ring on alignment, with magnifications shown by image size.

figures.label: Fig. 16.14
figures.caption_paraphrase: A Hubble Space Telescope image illustrating gravitational lensing.
figures.visual_description: A black-and-white deep-sky photograph dominated by many small galaxies: a bright foreground star with diffraction spikes near the top, a compact bright galaxy group in the centre, and a few spiral galaxies lower right. At this reproduction size, lensed arcs are not clearly identifiable.
figures.what_it_teaches: Lensing is a routine observational phenomenon in modern astronomy.

redesign.idea: Replace with a clearly lensed cluster image annotated with arcs and multiple images, with a slider that 'removes' the lens model to show reconstructed source positions.
redesign.interaction: Hover arcs to highlight counterpart images; toggle a mass map overlay including dark matter.

figures.label: Fig. 16.15
figures.caption_paraphrase: Radar ray passing the Sun between a planet and Earth.
figures.visual_description: Two concentric circles around a small Sun at the centre: the inner labelled Planet's orbit and the outer Earth's orbit. A straight line labelled Light ray (with an arrow) joins the planet on the inner circle at left to Earth on the outer circle at right, passing just above the Sun. A short perpendicular D from the Sun to the ray has a right-angle mark; radial labels D_P and D_E mark the orbit radii.
figures.what_it_teaches: Defines the closest approach D and the two leg lengths used in the round-trip time integral.

redesign.idea: Superior-conjunction radar-delay plotter.
redesign.interaction: Animate Earth and Venus in their orbits; plot excess delay versus date, showing the logarithmic spike (hundreds of microseconds) as the ray grazes the Sun, with gamma adjustable to show how the spike scales.

figures.label: Fig. 16.16
figures.caption_paraphrase: A marble on a flat sheet mimics straight-line motion in special relativity.
figures.visual_description: A shallow open box with a dark grey taut rubber sheet stretched over its top. A small marble sits near the right end of a straight track line drawn diagonally across the sheet. Labels: track of marble, marble, taut rubber sheet, box.
figures.what_it_teaches: Without a central mass, free motion is straight at constant speed.

redesign.idea: Combined with Fig. 16.17 in a single sheet simulator (see there).
redesign.interaction: Start with zero central weight: marbles launched in any direction travel straight.

figures.label: Fig. 16.17
figures.caption_paraphrase: With a weight in the centre, the marble orbits and its ellipse precesses.
figures.visual_description: The same box and sheet, now with a central weight sitting in a dimple from which fine radial crease lines spread. An elliptical marble track loops around the weight.
figures.what_it_teaches: A curved surface makes free paths curve into orbits; the book adds that the ellipse precesses.

redesign.idea: 3D dented-sheet simulator that deliberately contrasts three things: marble motion on a funnel under external gravity, true geodesics of the funnel with no gravity, and GR orbits.
redesign.interaction: Set weight (dent depth), launch speed and direction, friction on/off. Show that on-sheet orbits precess even without friction (because the effective force is not inverse-square) and that friction mainly causes inspiral; overlay the GR precession for comparison with the caution that the mechanism differs.

figures.label: Fig. 16.18
figures.caption_paraphrase: The Schwarzschild spatial slice embedded in Euclidean 3-space.
figures.visual_description: A square flat grid of concentric circles and radial lines that dips smoothly into a funnel at its centre; the funnel's sides become nearly vertical lines converging to a narrow throat far below.
