Axes x, y (horizontal) and z (vertical, dashed through the funnel) are drawn.
figures.what_it_teaches: Radial proper distances are stretched near the mass: the surface's induced metric reproduces (16.83); the throat corresponds to r = 2m.

redesign.idea: Build-your-own embedding: rings of circumference 2 pi r stacked so the slanted distance between neighbours equals the proper radial distance.
redesign.interaction: Slide m; a ruler tool measures proper distance along the surface between two circles and compares with the naive difference in r. Toggle 'upper half only' versus 'full Flamm paraboloid'.

figures.label: Fig. 16.19
figures.caption_paraphrase: Embedding geometry outside and inside a spherical star.
figures.visual_description: A wide gridded surface dips into a funnel as in Fig. 16.18, but the funnel stops at a rim labelled r = r_0, below which short vertical grid lines lead into a rounded, stippled bowl labelled star interior. A third leader line labelled r = 2m points into the lower part of this bowl, apparently marking where the vacuum funnel would otherwise have continued toward its throat.
figures.what_it_teaches: A real star replaces the deep funnel with a smooth bowl; the exterior matches Schwarzschild and the interior solution caps it, resembling the dented rubber sheet.

redesign.idea: Compactness slider for a uniform-density star embedded with Schwarzschild interior and exterior geometry.
redesign.interaction: Slide r_0/2m from large to about 9/8; the cap deepens and the exterior funnel lengthens, showing when the r = 2m throat would be exposed (black-hole preview).

figures.label: Fig. 16.20
figures.caption_paraphrase: Picturing light bending on the embedded geometry of a star.
figures.visual_description: The capped funnel surface of Fig. 16.19 seen obliquely, with an eye symbol at the lower-left corner and four small stars along the far (top) edge. From the eye, solid and dashed lines run across the dent toward the stars: a curved path bends around the rim of the depression, while dashed straight continuations point to the star labelled apparent position of star, displaced from the star labelled actual position of star.
figures.what_it_teaches: Geodesics on the curved spatial surface bend around the mass, so the star appears displaced; the book warns this captures only half the true deflection.

redesign.idea: Geodesic-on-surface tracer with a 'space-only versus space-time' toggle.
redesign.interaction: Shoot geodesics across the embedded surface and measure their deflection; compare with the full GR value, showing the surface gives 2m/D and the time part of the metric supplies the other 2m/D, linked to the (1 + gamma)/2 factor.

worked_examples.label: Inline: redshift in a static space-time (16.1)-(16.11)
worked_examples.problem: Find the frequency received by one static observer from an atomic clock held by another static observer in a general static metric, then specialize to the weak field and to light leaving the Sun.
worked_examples.method: Write proper time as sqrt(g_00) dx^0 for each clock; argue the world-time interval between crests is the same at both ends; divide; substitute g_00 = 1 + 2phi/c^2 and phi = -GM/r; insert solar radius and 1 AU.
worked_examples.key_insight: Staticity alone fixes the answer: no field equations, only the metric's time part.
worked_examples.result: nu_2/nu_1 = sqrt(g_00(x_1)/g_00(x_2)); Delta nu/nu = (phi_1 - phi_2)/c^2; about -2.12 x 10^-6 for the Sun.

worked_examples.label: Inline: GPS relativistic budget (16.12)
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the relative sizes of kinematic time dilation and gravitational frequency shift for a GPS satellite clock.
worked_examples.method: Use orbital speed of about 4 km/s for the special-relativistic factor and GM_e/(c^2 R_S) for the gravitational term; compare and convert to timing and distance errors.
worked_examples.key_insight: Both effects are fractions of order 10^-10 but accumulate; they must be corrected for metre-level navigation.
worked_examples.result: Book: gravitational term about twice the kinematic one, ~1 ns or 30 cm. Dossier check: kinematic v^2/2c^2 ~ 8e-11 and satellite potential GM/(c^2 R_S) ~ 1.7e-10 (ratio ~2, as stated, but the book's powers of ten are 100 times too large); the ground-to-orbit gravitational shift is ~5.3e-10 with the opposite sign to time dilation, giving a net satellite clock gain of ~38 microseconds per day.

worked_examples.label: Inline: Newtonian Kepler orbit via Binet's equation (16.14)-(16.25)
worked_examples.problem: Find the shape of the orbit of a particle under an inverse-square central force.
worked_examples.method: Show angular momentum conservation implies planar motion; resolve acceleration in polar coordinates; integrate the transverse equation; substitute u = 1/R with the chain rule; solve the resulting linear ODE.
worked_examples.key_insight: In the variable u(phi) the inverse-square problem becomes a forced harmonic oscillator, so conics fall out immediately.
worked_examples.result: l/R = 1 + e cos(phi - phi_0) with l = h^2/mu.

worked_examples.label: Inline: two-body reduction (16.26)-(16.29)
worked_examples.problem: Show two point masses in mutual gravitational attraction obey a one-body equation.
worked_examples.method: Subtract the two Newton's-second-law equations using the third law to get the equation for the relative vector.
worked_examples.key_insight: Only the total mass sets the orbit of the relative coordinate; the reduced mass multiplies both sides.
worked_examples.result: m r-double-dot = -m mu r-hat/r^2 with m = m_1 m_2/(m_1 + m_2), mu = G(m_1 + m_2).
concepts: Reduced mass and the two-body problem

worked_examples.label: Inline: Schwarzschild orbit equation (16.30)-(16.38)
worked_examples.problem: Derive the differential equation for the orbit u(phi) of a massive test particle in the Schwarzschild field.
worked_examples.method: Write the Lagrangian first integral 2K = 1; use the t, theta, phi Euler-Lagrange equations; show motion can be taken equatorial; integrate for k and h; substitute into 2K = 1; use u = 1/r and r-dot = -h du/dphi; differentiate once in phi.
worked_examples.key_insight: Ignorable coordinates give conserved k and h, and the Schwarzschild orbit equation is Binet's equation with one extra term 3mu^2.
concepts: Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass

worked_examples.label: Inline: perturbative perihelion advance (16.39)-(16.50)
worked_examples.problem: Solve the relativistic Binet equation to first order in the small parameter and find the perihelion shift per orbit.
worked_examples.method: Nondimensionalize; expand in epsilon = 3m^2/h^2; zeroth order is the Kepler conic; first-order forcing contains a resonant cos phi term; use trial solution with A, B phi sin phi, C cos 2phi; keep the growing term and combine with the cosine; convert with h^2 = m a (1 - e^2) and Kepler's third law.
worked_examples.key_insight: The growing phi sin phi term is not a failure but a phase drift: the ellipse returns to perihelion after 2 pi (1 + epsilon).
worked_examples.result: Delta phi = 6 pi GM/(c^2 a (1 - e^2)) per orbit = 24 pi^3 a^2/(c^2 T^2 (1 - e^2)); about 43 arcsec per century for Mercury (dossier check: epsilon ~ 8e-8, 0.104 arcsec per orbit, 415 orbits per century).

worked_examples.label: Inline: light deflection by the Sun (16.51)-(16.60)
worked_examples.problem: Find the angle through which a light ray passing a spherical mass at closest distance D is deflected.
worked_examples.method: Null version of the orbit equation; straight line u = sin(phi)/D at zeroth order; nondimensionalize with epsilon = 3m/D; solve the first-order equation forced by sin^2 phi; impose u = 0 at the two asymptotic directions phi = -epsilon_1 and pi + epsilon_2 with small-angle approximations; add.
worked_examples.key_insight: The integration constant C only tilts the picture and cancels in the sum of asymptote angles.
worked_examples.result: Delta phi = 4GM/(c^2 D), 1.75 arcsec at the solar limb.

worked_examples.label: Inline: radar echo time delay (16.61)-(16.75)
worked_examples.problem: Compute the round-trip coordinate time for a radar pulse from Earth to a planet on the far side of the Sun and back, and the excess over the flat-space value.
worked_examples.method: Null Lagrangian with conserved h and k; closest-approach condition fixes h^2/k^2; eliminate phi to get dt/dr; expand to first order in m; integrate each term from D to D_P and D_E (substitution r = D cosh u helps); double; approximate for D near the solar radius and D much smaller than orbital radii.
worked_examples.key_insight: The dominant delay is logarithmic in the geometry, so it is large (hundreds of microseconds) only when the ray grazes the Sun.
worked_examples.result: Delta T about 4GM/c^3 [ln(4 D_P D_E / D_S^2) + 1]; about 200 microseconds for Venus (book); dossier estimate about 250 microseconds at exact grazing.

worked_examples.label: Inline: PPN coefficients of the static spherical metric (16.76)-(16.82)
worked_examples.problem: Parametrize deviations from Schwarzschild in a general metric theory and express the three tests in terms of the parameters.
worked_examples.method: Use the only dimensionless radius c^2 r/GM; impose the Newtonian limit on A and flat-space limit on B; expand to post-Newtonian order; match to the isotropic PPN metric via r = rho + const; repeat the perturbation calculations (left as exercise).
worked_examples.key_insight: Light deflection and delay probe only gamma (spatial curvature), while perihelion advance also probes beta (non-linearity), so combining tests separates them.
worked_examples.result: A_2 = 2(beta - gamma), B_1 = 2gamma; perihelion factor (2 + 2gamma - beta)/3; deflection and delay factor (1 + gamma)/2.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Marble rolling on a taut rubber sheet dented by a central weight
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Flat sheet gives straight paths (special relativity); dented sheet gives orbits, even precessing ellipses, standing in for geodesics of the geometry around a mass. Then tied to the Schwarzschild embedding diagram.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Works only because Earth's gravity pulls the marble into the dent (circular as an explanation); curves space, not space-time, so light bending comes out half as large; friction and the non-inverse-square shape of the sheet produce spiralling and precession by mechanisms unrelated to GR; the embedding space has no physical meaning.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side: marble on a funnel under external gravity versus true geodesics on the same funnel with gravity switched off versus a GR orbit; a checklist of what matches and what does not.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Embedding diagram as a faithful picture of spatial distances
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Presented as the precise version of the rubber sheet: a surface in Euclidean 3-space whose surface distances equal the proper distances of the Schwarzschild equatorial slice.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only a 2D spatial slice at one time; points off the surface and the vertical direction mean nothing; misses the time-time metric part that dominates orbital dynamics and half of light bending.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ruler tool on the funnel measuring surface distance between circumference rings versus the difference in r.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Gravitational lens compared with an optical lens
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Mass focuses light like a lens, forming a caustic and multiple images; the contrast emphasized is that the gravitational version is achromatic.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A point-mass lens has no single focal point (deflection falls off as 1/D, opposite to a converging glass lens where outer rays bend more), and it can form multiple images of one source.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between a glass lens and a point-mass lens with the same ray bundle, showing focus versus caustic and dispersion versus none.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve (Wheeler's slogan)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Summarizes the lesson of the rubber sheet: geometry guides free motion, mass shapes geometry.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A slogan, not a mechanism; hides that 'how to curve' is governed by the field equations and that curvature is of space-time rather than space.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Ripples spreading on the rubber sheet when the central weight changes
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: Finite propagation speed of gravitational influence
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Contrasts GR's local, finite-speed propagation of changes in the field with Newtonian instantaneous action at a distance, previewing gravitational waves.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Rubber-sheet waves travel at a speed set by the sheet's tension and density, not c; real gravitational waves are transverse tidal strains, not vertical dents.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Wiggle the central mass and watch a ripple front expand while a distant marble responds only when the front arrives; compare with a Newtonian mode where it responds instantly.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Newtonian planetary perturbations acting like the relativistic extra term
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The authors observe that other planets perturb an orbit in a way similar in effect to the 3mu^2 term, which is why most of Mercury's precession is Newtonian and only a residual is relativistic.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Planetary perturbations vary with the configuration of the planets and are not a pure power-law in u; the GR term is universal and depends only on the Sun's mass.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Perihelion budget bar: precession of the equinoxes, each planet's pull, solar oblateness, GR residual.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational redshift is a test of Einstein's field equations or of the Schwarzschild solution specifically.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Any theory obeying the equivalence principle in a static field predicts it; the derivation uses only g_00 and staticity, not the field equations.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The textbook formula is usually written with the Schwarzschild g_00, and it was historically listed among the 'tests of GR'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: All of Mercury's perihelion advance is a relativistic effect.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The overwhelming majority is Newtonian (perturbations by other planets, plus the precession of the reference frame); GR accounts for the residual of about 43 arcsec per century.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Popular accounts quote 'Mercury's precession' without separating the tiny anomaly from the large total.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A gravitational lens behaves like a glass lens, with different colours focusing at different places.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Gravitational deflection is independent of frequency (achromatic) and depends only on the deflecting mass.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The name 'lens' and ray diagrams borrowed from optics.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The rubber-sheet or embedding picture of curved space gives the full light deflection.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Curvature of space alone gives only half; the other half comes from the time part of the metric (in PPN terms the '1' versus the 'gamma' in (1 + gamma)/2).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The embedding diagram looks like a complete picture of the geometry and rays visibly bend on it.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The third dimension of an embedding diagram (the depth of the funnel) is a real direction in space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the intrinsic geometry of the 2-surface has meaning; points off the surface and distances through the surrounding Euclidean space are not physical.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The picture is drawn in 3D and looks like a physical funnel into which things fall.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Changes in a mass are felt everywhere instantly, as in Newtonian gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In GR changes propagate as ripples in geometry at the speed of light.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newton's law contains no propagation delay, and it works so well in the solar system.
concepts: Finite propagation speed of gravitational influence

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Eddington's 1919 eclipse photographs decisively confirmed Einstein's prediction.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The measurements suffered from corona, systematic and emulsion problems; repeated eclipse campaigns scattered between 0.7 and 1.55 times the prediction, and precise confirmation came from radio interferometry.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The story is famous for its dramatic press coverage and Einstein's celebrity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: In GR, orbits around the Sun are closed ellipses just like Newton's, only slightly bigger or smaller.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The relativistic orbit is not closed: the ellipse's axis rotates by 2 pi epsilon each revolution, giving a rosette.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Kepler ellipses are so familiar, and the correction is tiny.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Newtonian gravity predicts no bending of light at all.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Massless light does move straight in the book's m = 0 limit, but a Newtonian corpuscle of any speed c is deflected by 2GM/(c^2 D), half the GR value; the factor of two is the real discriminator.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book's comment that the straight line agrees with Newtonian theory, and the idea that gravity only acts on massive things.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: In GPS both relativistic effects make the satellite clock run slow.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Orbital speed makes the satellite clock run slow (about 7 microseconds per day), but being higher in Earth's potential makes it run fast (about 45 microseconds per day); the net is a gain of about 38 microseconds per day.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book states that both effects make received signals slower, and 'time dilation' is associated with slowing.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The rubber-sheet marble's precession demonstrates the relativistic mechanism of perihelion advance.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The marble's orbit precesses because the sheet's shape gives a non-inverse-square effective force, and friction makes it spiral in; GR precession arises from the 3mu^2 term of the Schwarzschild orbit equation.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book attributes the marble's precession to friction and presents it as analogous to planets.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Shapiro delay is measured by comparing the actual travel time with a known flat-space travel time.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The flat-space distance is not independently known and depends on coordinates; experiments detect the characteristic time variation of echo delays as the ray's closest approach to the Sun changes near superior conjunction.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The derivation subtracts the m = 0 term and calls the remainder the excess delay.

thought_experiments.name: Gravitational perpetuum mobile
thought_experiments.setup: An endless chain between Earth and Sun carries excited atoms down on one side and ground-state atoms up on the other. At the bottom a device de-excites arriving atoms and mirrors the emitted light up to Earth to re-excite atoms there.
thought_experiments.lesson: Excited atoms are heavier, so the chain would turn forever unless the light reaching Earth has lost energy; energy conservation therefore requires gravitational redshift.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Energy ledger animation with a toggle that turns the redshift off and lets the energy counter run away.

thought_experiments.name: Two static clocks exchanging wave crests
thought_experiments.setup: Two observers at fixed spatial coordinates in a static space-time; one emits light crests, the other counts them against its own atomic clock.
thought_experiments.lesson: Time-translation symmetry forces equal world-time intervals, so the proper-time rates differ as sqrt(g_00), giving the redshift without the field equations.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Spacetime diagram in which the learner drags the second crest's world line and sees that any non-parallel choice would pile up crests over time.

thought_experiments.name: Vulcan: an unseen planet to explain Mercury
thought_experiments.setup: Suppose the 43 arcsec per century anomaly came from an undiscovered planet inside Mercury's orbit.
thought_experiments.lesson: A Newtonian fix requires unobserved matter; no such planet exists, and GR explains the anomaly with no free parameters (an instructive parallel to modern dark matter debates).
thought_experiments.app_idea: Add a hypothetical Vulcan with adjustable mass and orbit and try to reproduce 43 arcsec per century without disturbing other planets.

thought_experiments.name: Suddenly changing the central mass
thought_experiments.setup: The weight at the centre of the rubber sheet (or a star's mass) changes abruptly.
thought_experiments.lesson: In Newtonian theory the distant force changes at once; in GR the change spreads outward at light speed, the seed of gravitational waves.
concepts: Finite propagation speed of gravitational influence
thought_experiments.app_idea: Ripple-front animation with distant test particles responding only when the front arrives.

historical_notes.event: Proposed gravitational redshift as the first test of his theory.
historical_notes.significance: Although it later proved to test the equivalence principle, it remains foundational.

historical_notes.event: Discovery of recoil-free gamma emission giving extremely narrow lines.
historical_notes.significance: Made a laboratory redshift measurement over tens of metres feasible.

historical_notes.event: Measured the gravitational shift of gamma rays in a 22 m tower at Harvard, agreeing with the prediction to about 1%.
historical_notes.significance: First precise terrestrial confirmation of gravitational redshift.

historical_notes.event: A hydrogen maser clock flown on a Scout rocket to about 10,000 km was compared with a ground clock.
historical_notes.significance: Improved redshift accuracy by two orders of magnitude; the book notes the rocket's length nearly matched the Harvard tower's height.

historical_notes.event: Pendulum experiments comparing bobs of different materials, the precursors of the Eotvos torsion balance.
historical_notes.significance: Shows that universality of free fall has been tested with steadily improving precision for centuries before GR.

historical_notes.event: Torsion balance experiments around the turn of the twentieth century bounded |eta| below 5 x 10^-9.
historical_notes.significance: Established universality of free fall to high precision long before GR's tests.

historical_notes.event: Princeton and Moscow torsion-balance experiments using the Sun as source and Earth's rotation as modulation reached 10^-11 and 10^-12.
historical_notes.significance: Among the most precise null experiments in physics; later confirmed by Su et al. (1994).

historical_notes.event: Nineteenth-century astronomers proposed a planet, Vulcan, inside Mercury's orbit to explain the perihelion anomaly, with a reported sighting by a French astronomer.
historical_notes.significance: A cautionary tale of explaining anomalies with unseen matter; GR removed the need.

historical_notes.event: Led the eclipse expedition whose reported confirmation of light bending made Einstein famous, soon after World War I.
historical_notes.significance: Public turning point for GR, though the data were less clear-cut than claimed.

historical_notes.event: Reportedly said that had the observations disagreed he would have felt sorry for God, so confident was he in the theory.
historical_notes.significance: Illustrates the role of theoretical elegance and conviction.

historical_notes.event: Twin quasar 0957+561 A, B, 6 arcsec apart, identified as a gravitationally lensed pair produced by an intervening galaxy.

historical_notes.significance: Added a fourth classical test that later gave the best value of gamma.

historical_notes.event: Eddington introduced the parameter gamma in analysing the 1922 eclipse; Robertson and Schiff later added beta.
historical_notes.significance: Precursor of the PPN framework for comparing metric theories.

historical_notes.event: Proposed a scalar-tensor theory motivated by Mach's principle with an adjustable coupling omega.
historical_notes.significance: The archetypal rival that the PPN tests constrain.

historical_notes.event: Two LIGO detectors recorded gravitational waves matching a binary black-hole merger.
historical_notes.significance: Direct strong-field evidence complementing indirect binary-pulsar evidence.

applications_and_observations.details: Lines from the solar limb show a shift of the predicted order but are hard to interpret because of solar atmospheric motions; white dwarfs have larger shifts because of high mass-to-radius ratio (first measured 1954).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Delta nu/nu = -2.12 x 10^-6 for the Sun

applications_and_observations.details: Mossbauer gamma rays sent up a 22 m tower; the source was moved to Doppler-compensate the shift and restore resonant absorption.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Measured 0.997 +/- 0.009 of predicted 4.92 x 10^-15; lines sharp to 1 part in 10^12; gh/c^2 ~ 2.5 x 10^-15 (dossier estimate)

applications_and_observations.topic: Clocks on aircraft, rockets, satellites and Voyager
applications_and_observations.details: Rate comparisons of transported atomic clocks and spacecraft radio signals (Voyager I near Saturn, 1980) confirm the redshift at the 1% level; a 1976 rocket-borne maser reached a few parts in 10^4.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Altitude about 10,000 km; accuracy about 2 x 10^-4

applications_and_observations.details: Satellites at orbital radius about 2.7 x 10^4 km broadcast time and position; receivers triangulate from four or more satellites. Clock rates need both special-relativistic and gravitational corrections.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Book: gamma factor ~8 x 10^-9, gravitational term ~16 x 10^-9. Dossier estimate: v ~ 3.9 km/s, v^2/2c^2 ~ 8 x 10^-11 (-7 microseconds/day); ground-to-orbit gravitational shift ~5.3 x 10^-10 (+45 microseconds/day); net +38 microseconds/day, ~11 km/day of range error if uncorrected

applications_and_observations.topic: Torsion-balance tests of the weak equivalence principle
applications_and_observations.details: Eotvos (Earth's field, rotating apparatus), Dicke at Princeton and Braginsky in Moscow (Sun's field, Earth's rotation as modulation), confirmed by Su et al. 1994.

applications_and_observations.topic: Evidence for local Lorentz and position invariance
applications_and_observations.details: Refined Michelson-Morley tests, light-speed independence of source velocity (binary X-ray sources, pion decays), isotropy of light speed, clocks in rockets and satellites, spectral lines from distant galaxies, and comparison of Earth clocks with millisecond pulsar PSR 1937+21.
Newtonian n-body perturbations (Jupiter's mass is about 0.1% of the Sun's) explain most of the advance; the residual matches GR.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Residual ~43 arcsec/century (about 100 times the observational error pre-GR); GR 42.98; book quotes 42.98 +/- 5 (Lo et al. 2013; the uncertainty looks misprinted). Dossier estimate: epsilon ~ 8 x 10^-8, 0.104 arcsec per orbit, 415 orbits per century

applications_and_observations.topic: Residual precessions of Venus, Earth and Icarus
applications_and_observations.details: Table 16.1 compares GR predictions with observations; agreement is loose for Venus and Earth because the effects are small, but the 1971 Icarus measurement agrees well.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Venus 8.6 vs 8.4 +/- 4.8; Earth 3.8 vs 5.0 +/- 1.2; Icarus 10.3 vs 9.8 +/- 0.8 arcsec/century

applications_and_observations.details: The Hulse-Taylor pulsar's orbit precesses far faster than any planet's, in agreement with GR; orbital decay from gravitational radiation is treated in Chapter 21.

applications_and_observations.topic: Light deflection at the solar limb
applications_and_observations.details: Eclipse plates compared with night-sky plates of the same field; more than ten campaigns from 1919 onward scattered between 0.7 and 1.55 times the prediction; the book singles out the 2017 eclipse as among the most accurate.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Predicted 1.75 arcsec; 2017 eclipse: agreement with prediction to about 0.01% with measurement error under 3% (as printed); 3m/D ~ 6 x 10^-6 at the limb (book: order 10^-6)

applications_and_observations.topic: Radio deflection of quasars by VLBI
applications_and_observations.details: Long-baseline radio interferometry tracks quasar positions as the Sun passes near them, giving excellent agreement with GR (Lebach et al. 1995).
Double quasar 0957+561 (1980) lensed by a galaxy about a quarter of the way to the source; numerous Hubble lensing images; lensing maps mass whether luminous or dark, important for cosmology.

applications_and_observations.topic: Planetary radar and spacecraft time-delay measurements
applications_and_observations.details: Radar pulses bounced off Venus and Mercury and timed as the planets approach superior conjunction; Mariner and Viking spacecraft transponders improved accuracy.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Venus: ~200 microseconds delay, agreement within 5%; Viking 1976: better than 1%. Dossier estimate for a grazing Earth-Venus ray: ~250 microseconds

applications_and_observations.details: Gamma from time delay, then beta from Mercury's perihelion using that gamma; solar oblateness measurements show quadrupole effects too small to spoil the beta bound.

From 1919 eclipse through CMB (1965), pulsars (1967), Cygnus X-1 (1970), binary pulsar (1974) and its orbital decay (1978), double pulsar (2003), Gravity Probe B (2004), LIGO (2016 announcement), EHT black hole image (2019).

notation_and_conventions.convention: (+, -, -, -): timelike intervals have ds^2 > 0 and 2K = +1 along proper-time-parametrized timelike geodesics.
c = G = 1 in derivations with m = GM/c^2 (a length); results converted to non-relativistic units at the end using (15.55).
notation_and_conventions.notes: In §16.5 the same letter m denotes the particle's (reduced) mass; in §16.6 onward it is the geometric mass of the Sun.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Latin indices a, b run over space-time (0-3), Greek alpha over spatial coordinates; x^0 is called world time.
d/dt in the Newtonian section; d/dtau for timelike geodesics; derivative with respect to an affine parameter for null geodesics.
u = 1/r (or 1/R); u-tilde = h^2 u/m for orbits and u-tilde = D u for light, chosen to be of order one; primes denote d/dphi.
Small parameter 3m^2/h^2 for orbits (16.39) and 3m/D for light (16.54); epsilon_1 and epsilon_2 are asymptote angles in §16.7.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Three different meanings within two pages; Fig. 16.10 also labels the total deflection delta rather than Delta phi.

notation_and_conventions.convention: In §16.2, k is the ratio of received to emitted proper-time intervals (echoing the Bondi k-factor of Chapter 2); in §16.6 and §16.8, k is the conserved quantity (1 - 2m/r) t-dot.
Newtonian potential in §16.2 (phi_1, phi_2); azimuthal angle from §16.5 onward.
h angular momentum per unit mass; e eccentricity (upright roman e in the book); l semi-latus rectum; a semi-major axis; T orbital period.
D closest approach of a ray to the Sun; D_P planet orbital radius; D_E Earth orbital radius; D_S solar radius. R_S in §16.2 means GPS orbital radius, not Schwarzschild radius.
r-tilde = c^2 r/GM; A_2, B_1 expansion coefficients; rho isotropic radius; beta, gamma PPN parameters; Delta phi_P and Delta phi_L for perihelion and light-deflection angles.
Key results are printed on grey shaded panels; on the pages checked these include (16.8), (16.9), (16.15), (16.19), (16.23), (16.25), (16.38), (16.47), (16.51), (16.58) and (16.60).

notable.summary: Explain why angular momentum conservation gives the areal-rate law when h is non-zero, and describe the motion when h vanishes.
notable.why_notable: The h = 0 case (radial plunge) is a useful edge case the text skips.

notable.summary: Express the Newtonian orbital energy in polar and then u variables and use the conic solution to identify the semi-latus rectum and eccentricity in terms of E and h.
notable.why_notable: Connects eccentricity to energy, which later parallels k^2 - 1 in the relativistic first-order equation (16.37).

notable.summary: Show the centre of mass moves uniformly, work in its rest frame, describe both bodies' orbits, explain how Kepler's laws change, and derive the period in terms of the Sun's mass.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the Kepler third-law relation needed to reach (16.50).

notable.summary: Rewrite the perihelion shift entirely in terms of semi-major axis, period and eccentricity, eliminating the central mass.
notable.why_notable: Shows why short-period eccentric orbits like Mercury's are the best laboratories.

notable.summary: Recast equatorial timelike Schwarzschild motion as a one-dimensional energy equation with an effective potential, locate its turning points, decide which circular orbits are stable, and show the innermost stable one is at r = 6m with h^2 = 12m^2.
notable.why_notable: The ISCO is central to accretion-disc physics and black-hole imaging, and is the strongest bridge from this chapter to Part D.

notable.summary: Show that light can circle a Schwarzschild mass on a circular orbit at r = 3m.
notable.why_notable: Introduces the photon sphere, which sets the size of black-hole shadows.

notable.summary: Fill in the Shapiro-delay algebra: fix the turning-point constants, derive and expand the radial coordinate speed, and integrate the three terms (hint: a cosh substitution) to obtain the round-trip time.
notable.why_notable: The most computation-heavy derivation of the chapter; it exposes where the logarithm originates.

notable.summary: Assuming the areal radius differs from the isotropic radius by a constant plus decaying terms, compare the two metric forms and show A_2 = 2(beta - gamma) and B_1 = 2 gamma.
notable.why_notable: Makes the PPN parameters concrete; doing it also reveals the sign misprint in (16.79).

difficulty.notes: The mathematics is mostly ODEs, perturbation theory and elementary integrals rather than tensor calculus, and every step is shown or set as an exercise, so an undergraduate can follow. The conceptual load comes from separating what each test really probes (equivalence principle versus metric versus PPN parameters) and from the embedding-diagram caveats. Novices are slowed by overloaded symbols (m, k, phi, epsilon), a dense §16.9 that states results without derivation and has typos in its key equations, and some unreliable numbers in the GPS paragraph and chronology.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive gravitational redshift from energy conservation with a perpetual-motion bucket chain before any metric appears.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners already trust energy conservation and E = mc^2; the paradox makes the redshift feel inevitable rather than exotic, and it previews that the effect needs only the equivalence principle.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Animated machine with a 'turn redshift off' switch that sends an energy meter into runaway, then an equation panel showing the required frequency loss equals the potential energy per unit mass-energy.

teaching_gems.gem: In a static space-time, count crests: world-time intervals are equal at both ends, so frequency ratios come only from sqrt(g_00).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces vague 'clocks tick slower' talk with a clean symmetry argument on a spacetime diagram and separates coordinate time from proper time.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Draggable two-observer spacetime diagram where parallel signal world lines and tick spacing update with the local g_00.

teaching_gems.gem: Do Kepler with Binet's equation first, so GR's orbit equation is 'the same plus 3mu^2'.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The novelty is isolated in one term, whose size (3v^2/c^2 relative) can be estimated before solving anything.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Equation morph: Newtonian Binet equation with a slider fading in the 3mu^2 term while the orbit plot changes from closed ellipse to rosette.

teaching_gems.gem: Turn the growing secular term e epsilon phi sin phi into cos[phi(1 - epsilon)]: the 'blow-up' is really a slowly rotating ellipse.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Converts a formal perturbation artifact into a vivid geometric picture and teaches a transferable resummation idea.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Plot the naive first-order solution, the resummed one and the exact numerical orbit for exaggerated epsilon; the naive one visibly diverges after a few orbits.

teaching_gems.gem: Get the deflection angle from where the perturbed ray reaches infinity: u = 0 at two slightly shifted angles whose sum is the bending.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Avoids trajectory integration; the arbitrary constant cancels, showing the answer is independent of orientation choices.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Interactive ray with asymptote handles; learner drags C and sees epsilon_1 and epsilon_2 trade off while their sum stays 4m/D.

teaching_gems.gem: Reframe old tests as measurements of beta and gamma: deflection and delay see (1 + gamma)/2, perihelion sees (2 + 2 gamma - beta)/3.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows how a theory is tested against a family of rivals, not just against Newton, and explains why several different tests are needed.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Beta-gamma plane with shaded allowed bands from each experiment; sliders for Brans-Dicke omega move a theory point along the gamma axis.

teaching_gems.gem: Tie the embedding diagram's 'half' light bending to the PPN split: space curvature gives the gamma half, the time part of the metric gives the other.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Combines the book's caution in §16.11 with the formula of §16.9 into one memorable fact that corrects the rubber-sheet intuition.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Toggle 'curve space only', 'curve time only', 'both' in a ray tracer and watch the deflection read 2m/D, 2m/D, 4m/D.

teaching_gems.gem: Present the Einstein equivalence principle as three separately testable clauses, each paired with experiments, then derive metric-theory postulates.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes the logical bridge from lab experiments to 'gravity is geometry' explicit and auditable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Card-sort activity: drag experiments (Eotvos, Michelson-Morley, Pound-Rebka, pulsar timing) onto the clause they test; completed columns unlock the metric-theory postulates.

teaching_gems.gem: Use GPS as the everyday stake: two opposite relativistic clock effects that must be engineered away.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects abstract potentials to a technology learners use daily and gives a concrete scale for tiny fractional shifts (with the numbers corrected).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Satellite-altitude slider plotting kinematic, gravitational and net clock-rate offsets in microseconds per day, marking the altitude where they cancel (about 1.5 Earth radii from the centre).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: GPS paragraph: the printed fractional effects (gamma factor ~8 x 10^-9, GM_e/(c^2 R_S) ~16 x 10^-9) are about 100 times too large; 'radial speed' should be orbital speed; the relevant gravitational term is the ground-to-orbit potential difference (~5.3 x 10^-10); and the two effects act in opposite directions, not both slowing the received signal.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Wrong orders of magnitude and wrong sign reasoning for the most familiar application; learners checking the arithmetic will be confused.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Teach with corrected values: -7 microseconds/day kinematic, +45 microseconds/day gravitational, net +38 microseconds/day for the satellite clock relative to the ground.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. (16.76) prints B(r) dt^2 instead of B(r) dr^2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A learner copying the metric will get a degenerate line element.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the corrected form and cross-check against (16.78).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. (16.79), recovered from the page render, has the spatial factor as (1 - 2 gamma GM/c^2 rho) and omits c^2 dt^2 on the first term; the sign must be plus to reproduce Schwarzschild and B_1 = 2 gamma.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Exercise 16.18 cannot be completed consistently with the printed sign, and the definition of gamma is garbled.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the PPN metric with (1 + 2 gamma GM/c^2 rho) and verify it against the isotropic Schwarzschild metric expanded to first order.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. (16.82) has D_S instead of D_S^2 inside the logarithm, disagreeing with (16.75).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Numerical evaluation gives a wrong (and dimensionful) argument of the log.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use ln(4 D_E D_P / D_S^2) and point out that a logarithm's argument must be dimensionless.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Symbol overloading: m is reduced mass in §16.5 but GM/c^2 in §16.6; k is the redshift ratio in §16.2 but a conserved quantity in §16.6; phi is potential then angle; epsilon has three meanings; Fig. 16.10 labels the deflection delta.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Easy to import a formula with the wrong meaning, for example treating h^2 = m a (1 - e^2) as involving the planet's mass.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: In the app, rename: M_geom or r_g for GM/c^2, E-tilde for k, Phi for potential, epsilon_orb and epsilon_light, and delta for deflection.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Quoted precisions are dated or implausible: Mercury's anomaly '42.98 +/- 5' arcsec/century (an uncertainty larger than Table 16.1's), gamma = 1.000 +/- 0.002 (Cassini 2003 gives about 2 x 10^-5), beta +/- 0.003 (now of order 10^-4 or better).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Underestimates how precisely GR is now tested.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Quote current bounds from Will's latest Living Review alongside the book's values.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The rubber-sheet model is presented without noting that it uses Earth's gravity to explain gravity, and marble precession is attributed to friction rather than to the sheet's non-Keplerian shape.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Reinforces the popular but circular picture and misattributes the mechanism of precession.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show geodesics on the dented surface with no external gravity (they deflect but do not orbit) and then add the time part of the metric to get orbits.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Shapiro 'excess delay' compares coordinate times with an m = 0 value in the same coordinates, which is not directly measurable; Earth-clock proper time and the observed time variation near conjunction are not discussed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think a flat-space travel time is known independently.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Emphasize that the observable is the logarithmic spike in delay as the closest approach D changes over days.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The perturbation solution (16.46) is called general but omits homogeneous first-order terms, and the secular expansion is valid only while epsilon phi is small; resummation into (16.47) is asserted with '(check)'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Strong students may worry about validity after many orbits; weaker ones may miss why the resummation is legitimate.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show numerically that the exact orbit follows the resummed form for thousands of orbits, and mention the Poincare-Lindstedt method.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Chronology inconsistencies and typos: the 1976 rocket test and the '1979 Scout rocket maser' entry appear to be one experiment; LIGO dated 2016 in the list but 2015 in the introduction (detection 2015, announcement 2016); Gravity Probe B flew in 2004 but reported in 2011; 'Hughs-Drever' and 'Shaprio' misspelled.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor, but undermines trust in the historical data.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use a curated timeline with both event and publication dates.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eotvos torque (16.13) is schematic: it lacks the mass factor and mixes a vector magnitude with a product of vectors (should be a scalar triple product).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Dimensional check fails; learners cannot estimate torques.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write the torque as roughly eta m l (g x k) . i with m the mass of each body, and discuss the horizontal component of g that actually drives it.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Pound-Rebka's quoted 'predicted shift of 4.92 x 10^-15' is twice gh/c^2 for the tower; it corresponds to the combined difference between upward and downward runs, which the text does not explain.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A learner computing gh/c^2 gets 2.5 x 10^-15 and suspects an error.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Explain the up/down reversal technique used to cancel systematic offsets.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Newtonian comparison for light bending is only 'straight line when m = 0'; the half-value Newtonian corpuscle deflection (Soldner) is not mentioned, even though the factor of two is what the eclipses tested.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Misses why the 1919 result mattered: distinguishing 0.87 from 1.75 arcsec.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add the Newtonian 2GM/(c^2 D) result and link its missing half to spatial curvature (gamma).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The statement that the ten PPN parameters relate to the ten independent metric components is loose; they are coefficients of specific post-Newtonian potentials in the metric.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Could suggest a one-to-one parameter/component map.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'ten coefficients multiplying standard post-Newtonian potentials' and list their physical roles.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed precision statements that cannot be right as written: the 1976 maser result is said to differ from theory by 'less than one part in 2 x 10^-4' (should read an agreement at the 2 x 10^-4 level), and the 2017 eclipse is said to agree to about 0.01% while carrying an error below 3%.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners who take the numbers literally will be confused about what fractional precision was actually achieved.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Quote the rocket test as confirming the redshift to about 2 parts in 10^4, and present the 2017 eclipse as a percent-level measurement consistent with GR.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If you built a machine that dropped heavier excited atoms toward the Sun and sent their light back up, what would stop it running forever?' Let the learner find the redshift before any formula.

Order: redshift (needs only equivalence principle) -> Eotvos and the Einstein equivalence principle (why geometry) -> Kepler via Binet -> GR orbit equation -> precession -> light bending -> time delay -> PPN -> rubber sheet with caveats.

Before solving the relativistic Binet equation, ask the learner to estimate the size of the 3mu^2 term relative to m/h^2 for Mercury (about 3v^2/c^2, roughly 10^-7). This builds perturbative intuition.
Check understanding of the secular term by asking: 'The first-order correction grows without bound; does that mean the orbit blows up?' Expect the rotating-ellipse answer.

Common question: 'Why is the redshift not a test of GR?' Answer: any metric theory with the equivalence principle gives the same leading-order result; it constrains local position invariance, not the field equations.

Common question: 'Why is light bent twice the Newtonian amount?' Use the PPN factor (1 + gamma)/2: time curvature gives the Newtonian-like half, space curvature (gamma = 1) the other half; relate to the embedding-diagram caveat.
Common question: 'How do we know the flat-space travel time for the Shapiro test?' Explain that experiments watch the delay change as the ray's closest approach sweeps past the Sun.
When the learner meets m in §16.6, confirm they know it is GM/c^2 (1.48 km for the Sun), not the planet's mass as in §16.5.
Give corrected GPS numbers (-7, +45, net +38 microseconds per day) if the book's GPS paragraph comes up, and flag the sign issue explicitly.

For advanced learners, assign the effective-potential exercise (ISCO at 6m) and the photon sphere (3m) as a bridge to black holes; for beginners, stay with numerical evaluations of 43 arcsec/century, 1.75 arcsec and ~200 microseconds.
Quick numeric checks to ask for: GM/(c^2 R_sun) ~ 2 x 10^-6; 4GM/(c^2 R_sun) in arcsec; 4GM_sun/c^3 ~ 20 microseconds as the delay scale.

When using the rubber sheet, ask the learner what makes the marble roll into the dent. Use the answer (Earth's gravity) to motivate why the analogy is circular and why space-time, not just space, must curve.
Use the beta-gamma plane to explain how one experiment constrains a line and two experiments pin a point; ask which tests are insensitive to beta.
Mention that modern bounds are far tighter than the book's values (Cassini gamma ~ 10^-5) so learners appreciate current precision.
